**Status: Sweden has no law implementing the EU Pay Transparency Directive. The user cannot rely on the directive's new rights in Sweden.** This note is time-sensitive and must be checked again before it is relied on.

chunks.heading: What the directive is
chunks.text: The EU Pay Transparency Directive (2023/970) was adopted in spring 2023 with a transposition deadline of **7 June 2026**. Among other things, it would give job applicants the right to information about starting pay or pay range, and limit employers asking about pay history; it would also give employees rights to information about pay levels and require employers to report pay gaps. These are what the directive provides. They do not apply in Sweden as long as no Swedish law implements them.

chunks.heading: What happened in Sweden (checked 2026-11-21)
chunks.text:
| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| Spring 2023 | The directive adopted. The government says it voted against it |
| January and March 2026 | A draft implementation was prepared. On 11 March 2026 the government proposed entry into force on 1 January 2027 |
| 26 March 2026 | The government stated that it does not currently intend to submit a bill on the directive to the Riksdag |
| 7 June 2026 | The EU transposition deadline passed without a Swedish law |
| 4 and 8 June 2026 | The government told the Equality Ombudsman (DO) to continue preparatory work and promote employers' pay surveys; DO reports by **1 November 2027**. The government says it will work to postpone the date and renegotiate parts of the directive |

Sources checked on 2026-11-21 agree that no implementing law exists. Almega (published 21 August 2026, updated 16 November 2026) reports that the government has withdrawn its proposal and that no new one exists; no new Swedish law is expected in 2026 and probably not in 2027, and the earliest possible entry into force is the first half of 2027 with a later date more likely. Unionen likewise states that the Swedish legislative work was stopped in March 2026 and that there is no applicable law. Whether public employers must already apply parts of the directive since 7 June 2026 is debated and not settled; do not tell public-sector users they have these rights.

chunks.heading: What still applies in Sweden
chunks.text:
- The Discrimination Act requires employers to prevent pay discrimination and to carry out an annual **pay survey** (*lönekartläggning*) (Pay-Survey-Lonekartlaggning, Discrimination-Act-and-Pay-Equity).
- Nothing in Swedish law, as far as found, requires an employer to publish a pay range in a job ad or to tell an applicant the pay before an interview. Some employers do so voluntarily.
- The ban on employers asking about pay history that the directive provides is not a Swedish rule today. The user may still **decline to answer** and give a range instead (What-Is-Your-Current-Salary, RULE-019, RULE-053).

chunks.heading: How the coach uses this
chunks.text:
- Never tell a user that they have a **legal right** to a pay range or to refuse to answer about pay, or that an employer must publish pay ranges. Say it is not required by Swedish law today, and that it is still reasonable to ask: "Can you share the range for the role?" (What-Are-Your-Expectations)
- If a recruiter says "we are required by the new law", ask which law and treat it with care; the user may check with DO or their union.
- For the pay survey and equal-pay rights that do apply, see Pay-Survey-Lonekartlaggning.
- Say that the law may change, and that the status was checked on 2026-11-21.

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: Always check the government's page, DO and the Swedish Gender Equality Agency before relying on this note. If a Swedish law is passed, rewrite this note and the notes linked above.
A probation employment (*provanställning*) is a fixed-term trial for a person not yet tested in the role.

chunks.heading: What the statute and sources say (checked 2026-11-21)
chunks.text:
- **Length:** at most six months (6 §). A collective agreement can allow exceptions (Naturvetarna).
- **Ends or converts:** if either side does not want the employment to continue, notice must be given by the end of the probation. If no notice is given it becomes **permanent** (6 §).
- **Early end:** unless otherwise agreed, probation may be ended before the end of the period (6 §).
- **Employer's advance notice (31 §):** when the employer plans to end the probation early or not convert it, it must tell the employee at least **two weeks** ahead; a union-affiliated employee's local union is told at the same time, and both have the right to a consultation.
- **Protection:** no employment protection applies during the trial (Naturvetarna).

chunks.heading: How the coach uses this
chunks.text:
- Ask whether a probation applies, how long, and whether pay or terms differ during and after it. Do not assume lower pay in the probation.
- Suggest asking for a short probation, a dated review before the end, and agreed criteria for conversion (Propose-a-Dated-Review); this is advice on how to ask, not a statement of what employers accept.
- Get the length, the end date and the terms in writing (A-Accepting-and-Confirming-in-Writing).
- If the user is on probation and wants a raise, say that the risk of asking is judged by the user; the coach does not claim how employers react.

chunks.heading: Swedish example lines
chunks.text: - "Hur lång är provanställningen, och vad krävs för att den ska övergå i tillsvidare?" (How long is the probation, and what is needed for it to become permanent?)

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Assuming probation ends on its own into a permanent post without checking the notice rules.
- Accepting an open-ended probation description without an end date.

The Working Hours Act (*arbetstidslagen*) sets limits on working time. Pay is not set by it (Overtime-Compensation).

chunks.heading: What the statute says (checked 2026-11-21)
chunks.text:
| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Ordinary hours (5 §) | At most 40 hours a week; averaging up to 40 over up to four weeks is allowed where the work requires it |
| Overtime limits (8, 8 a §) | General overtime up to 48 hours per four weeks or 50 per month and 200 a year; extra overtime up to 150 more a year with special reasons (Overtime-Compensation) |
| Daily rest (13 §) | At least 11 consecutive hours in every 24 hours; this should include midnight to 5 a.m. unless the work requires otherwise |
| Weekly rest (14 §) | At least 36 consecutive hours in every seven days, preferably including a weekend |
| Breaks (15 §) | The employer sets them in advance; no more than five hours of work in a row without a break |
| Night work (13 a §) | Averages no more than 8 hours per 24 hours over a reference period of up to four months; night is 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. |

Collective agreements can deviate from several of these rules.

chunks.heading: How the coach uses this
chunks.text:
- Ask for `weekly_hours` and whether the pay is for full-time hours.
- When flexibility is part of the package (hours, remote days), ask how it is written: in the contract, in an agreement or in a policy that can change.
- For hourly or part-time conversions, use the engine; do not do the sums in the reply.
- The coach does not say whether a given schedule breaks the law; for that the user asks their union or the Swedish Work Environment Authority.

chunks.heading: Swedish example lines
chunks.text: - "Hur många timmar per vecka gäller tjänsten, och hur regleras flextid och övertid?" (How many hours a week apply to the post, and how are flexitime and overtime regulated?)

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Comparing two salaries without comparing weekly hours.
- Assuming the 40-hour limit applies unchanged where an agreement deviates.


*This note explains the rules so the coach can help the user ask the right questions. It is not legal advice; for a dispute or a contract question, the user should ask their union or a lawyer.*

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: Check the statute and the user's agreement.

Some agreements do not give a central amount for raises. They set a framework, and the pay increase is decided locally, between the employer and each employee, or the employer and the local union. This gives more room for individual negotiation, and also less protection from a general increase.

chunks.heading: What changes for the user
chunks.text:
- **No automatic raise.** There may be no general increase, so the user needs to ask and show their case at the yearly review (Salary-Review-Process).
- **The reference is the market and the user's own value**, not a pot or a percentage (Use-Market-Data).
- **The employer's criteria matter.** Ask what they are and which are weighted most (Local-and-Individual-Pay-Setting).
- **Timing matters.** The decision often follows the employer's own budget cycle (Typical-Timing-and-Budgets).

chunks.heading: How the coach uses this
chunks.text:
1. Establish which kind of agreement applies (slot `collective_agreement`, `pay_pool_norm`).
2. If there is no pool, treat the discussion as an individual negotiation with a framework around it (Local-and-Individual-Pay-Setting).
3. Build the case as in path B: results, scope, market range, timing (B-Evidence-Builder).
4. Where the agreement sets minimums or pension, treat those as fixed and focus on what is open.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Waiting to be offered a raise.
- Using a general percentage as the target.
- Not asking whether the union can help with the local process.

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: Whether a given agreement has a pool is a fact about that agreement. Check the text or ask HR or the union.

A collective agreement (*kollektivavtal*) is a written agreement between an employers' organisation (or a single employer) and a trade union about pay and other terms of employment. In Sweden it is the main way pay and conditions are set. For the coach it answers the first question in any pay discussion: **how much is already decided, and how much is left to negotiate?**

chunks.heading: Key facts (checked 2026-11-21)
chunks.text:
- **Coverage is high.** In 2025, 88% of employees aged 18 to 68 were covered by a collective agreement (same as 2024): 83% in the private sector, and all public-sector employees. Union membership was 66% of employees aged 15 to 74 (Public-vs-Private-Sector). Source: Medlingsinstitutet, 2025.
- **Agreements vary a lot.** They range from purely local pay setting to fixed general increases. About 73% of employees are covered by central agreements that set the pay pool, according to Medlingsinstitutet's 2025 report (Local-and-Individual-Pay-Setting, Agreements-Without-Fixed-Pool).
- **Many agreements also cover** pension, insurance, working time, extra vacation, notice periods and overtime rules. Which of these are fixed depends on the agreement (Occupational-Pension, Working-Hours).
- **The employer decides whether it is bound.** An employer is bound if it is a member of the employers' organisation that signed the agreement, or has signed its own agreement with the union.

chunks.heading: Points to check for the user (not to assume)
chunks.text:
| Question | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Is there an agreement at this employer? Which one? | Sets floors, pension and the rules for pay setting (slot `collective_agreement`) |
| Does it set a pay scale or only a framework? | A scale limits room on base pay; a framework leaves more to the individual |
| Is there a local pay pool or review process? | Where individual raises come from (Local-and-Individual-Pay-Setting) |
| Which terms are fixed (pension, vacation, notice, overtime)? | These are the terms that cannot be traded |

Generally, an employer bound by an agreement applies it to all employees in the covered work, whether or not they are union members. Verify this for the specific agreement and workplace.

chunks.heading: How the coach uses this
chunks.text:
- Ask early whether there is an agreement (slot `collective_agreement`). If the user does not know, explain how to find out: the employment contract, HR, or the union.
- If one applies, move the discussion to **placement** within the scale, local pay setting and the terms that are still open (Fixed-Scale-or-Agreement, Pay-Set-by-Agreement).
- Never state what a specific agreement says unless the user has given it or the researcher has returned it with a source. Say that the agreement text should be checked.
- Where no agreement exists, individual pay and terms are negotiated more freely, and the market range matters more.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Assuming "there is an agreement" means no room at all.
- Assuming a union-member status changes whether the agreement applies; check.
- Quoting percentages or levels from memory.

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: Coverage figures are for 2025 and change yearly. Agreement terms change in each bargaining round. Check the current agreement text and Medlingsinstitutet's latest statistics.

*Märket* is the pay-increase level set by the first agreements in the internationally exposed industry. The rest of the labour market uses it as a guide for general increases and for the size of local pay pools. It affects what employers say they can afford at a yearly review.

chunks.heading: Key facts (checked 2026-11-21)
chunks.text:
- Medlingsinstitutet (the Swedish National Mediation Office) describes the Swedish model as one where the first agreements reached in industry set the norm ("de först träffade avtalen inom industrin utgör normen"), and where mediators do not support deals that conflict with a well-functioning wage formation.
- **Industriavtalet 2025:** a two-year agreement signed around 31 March to 1 April 2025, running from April 2025 to March 2027. The total cost increase (the *kostnadsmärke*) is **6.4% over 24 months: 3.4% in year one and 3.0% in year two**. Part of the value is set aside for non-wage items such as reduced working time and partial pension, so average wage increases differ somewhat.
- In 2025, 549 agreements were signed; the renegotiated central agreements cover about 3.4 million employees.
- The industry agreement runs to March 2027, so a new bargaining round is due around then. Check the new figures when it happens.

chunks.heading: What it means in a salary talk
chunks.text:
- An employer may say "the norm is X%". That is a **general guideline for raises**, not a rule for an individual's pay and not for a new hire's starting salary.
- It helps the user predict the **size of the pot** at a yearly review (Salary-Review-Process) and what the employer may offer by default.
- The user's own case rests on evidence of value, scope and market data, not on the norm (Use-Market-Data).

chunks.heading: How the coach uses this
chunks.text:
- When the user hears "the budget is the norm", ask what the norm covers, who decides placement, and whether individual increases above it are possible (Budget-Is-Fixed).
- Do not quote the percentage for a sector other than industry without checking the sector's own agreement.
- Note the reference period; the figures above apply to the 2025 to 2027 round.

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: New rounds replace these figures. Check Medlingsinstitutet.

Even where a collective agreement applies, an individual's pay is often set locally: at the workplace, between the employer and either the local union or the employee. How much is decided locally varies by agreement, from a fixed general increase for everyone to purely local pay setting.

chunks.heading: Common models
chunks.text:
| Model | What it means in practice |
|---|---|
| **General increase** | A fixed percentage or amount for everyone; little individual room |
| **Pay pool (*pott*) with local negotiation** | The agreement gives a total amount; the employer and the local union, or the employer and each employee, decide how to distribute it |
| **Local pay setting only** | The agreement sets a framework and principles; pay is decided locally and individually |
| **Individual pay setting** | The employer sets pay individually, often with set criteria and a yearly *lönesamtal* |

Which model applies depends on the specific agreement; do not assume (Collective-Agreements).

chunks.heading: What to find out
chunks.text:
- How is the yearly pay review run, and when (Salary-Review-Process, Typical-Timing-and-Budgets)?
- Is there a pool, and who decides the distribution (the manager, HR, the union)?
- What criteria does the employer use (role, results, market, skills)?
- Does the user's union represent them in local negotiation, or does the user negotiate directly (Unions-and-Their-Role)?

chunks.heading: How the coach uses this
chunks.text:
- Path B: tailor the evidence and the ask to the criteria and the timing (B-Evidence-Builder, B-Timing-and-Budget-Cycle).
- If the manager says "there is only X% for everyone", ask how the pool is distributed and whether individual placement can differ (Pay-Set-by-Agreement).
- Do not assume the pool is fixed for every individual; ask.
- The numbers are the user's own plus the researcher's data; never present a generic percentage as the user's entitlement.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Treating a pool as an entitlement to the full percentage.
- Raising pay after the pay-setting window has closed.
- Negotiating alone when a union is entitled to represent the user locally, without checking.

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: The model in each agreement changes between rounds. Check the current agreement.

Pay is set within a framework in both sectors, but the room, the process and the openness differ.

| Aspect | Public sector | Private sector |
|---|---|---|
| Collective agreement | All employees covered (2025) | 83% covered (2025) |
| Pay setting | Central agreements, then local negotiation or set pay principles | Varies from general increases to local and individual pay setting |
| Pay information | Salary documents of authorities are normally public documents (Public-Access-to-Salary-Info) | Not covered by the public-access principle |
| Room for individual negotiation | Often limited by grades, scales and set principles | Often wider, but depends on agreement and employer |
| Typical levers | Placement in grade, role definition, development, schedule | Base, bonus, pension, flexibility, title |

Coverage figures are for 2025 from Medlingsinstitutet (Collective-Agreements).

chunks.heading: How the coach uses this
chunks.text:
- Ask whether the employer is public or private and which agreement applies (slots `employer_type`, `collective_agreement`).
- Public sector: focus the argument on **placement** and the role definition, and on other terms. The pay level is often visible, so the user can look at comparable roles (Public-Access-to-Salary-Info).
- Private sector: more room, so the market range and the evidence of value carry more weight (Use-Market-Data).
- Municipal companies and state-owned companies may be treated differently in public-access terms; do not generalise.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Assuming every public role has a fixed price list.
- Assuming a private employer has no agreement.
- Using public pay figures as the user's target without regard for the role.

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: Sector terms and the details of public access change. Check the sources.

Unions negotiate the collective agreements and, in many workplaces, take part in local pay setting and in the employer's pay survey. 66% of employees aged 15 to 74 were union members in 2025 (Medlingsinstitutet). For the user, the union is a source of information, advice and sometimes representation.

chunks.heading: What unions typically do
chunks.text:
- **Negotiate agreements** with employer organisations (Collective-Agreements).
- **Take part locally**: a local representative (*förtroendeman*) may negotiate with the employer about pay setting, depending on the agreement (Local-and-Individual-Pay-Setting).
- **Take part in the pay survey** (*lönekartläggning*) as part of the employer's work on active measures (Pay-Survey-Lonekartlaggning).
- **Advise members** on offers, contracts and pay, and often publish salary statistics. Check what the user's own union offers.
- **Pursue pay-discrimination matters** together with the Equality Ombudsman (Discrimination-Act-and-Pay-Equity).

chunks.heading: How the coach uses this
chunks.text:
- Ask whether the user is a union member and which union (a short, optional question, never required). Many unions provide advice and salary statistics to members.
- Suggest the union as a **source** for market data and agreement details, not as a substitute for the user's own case (Use-Market-Data).
- Where the user's union has local representation, mention that the user can ask whether the representative is part of the local pay process.
- Never give legal advice. For a dispute or a suspected breach, point to the union or a lawyer (Boundaries-and-Ethics).
- Do not assume membership; many users are not members.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Assuming the union will negotiate the user's own number.
- Assuming non-members have no access to the agreement terms.
- Skipping the union's statistics because "they are only for members" without checking what is public.

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: Union services and membership terms differ by union and change. Check the union's own pages.

The employer pays **employer contributions** (*arbetsgivaravgifter*) on top of the gross salary: **31.42% in 2026** for employees aged 24 to 67. So the employer's cost of a raise is larger than the raise itself. Understanding this helps the user see why "the budget" matters and how to frame a request (Perspective-Taking).

chunks.heading: What an extra krona of gross costs
chunks.text:
- **Employer contributions:** 31.42% of the gross increase, so each 1,000 SEK extra a month costs about 1,314 SEK a month (computed).
- **Other costs that follow the salary** (depending on the agreement and the employer): occupational pension contributions, holiday pay and supplements, and insurance premiums (Occupational-Pension, Vacation, Insurances). The amount depends on the agreement; do not guess.
- **Temporary reduction for young employees:** for those born 2003 to 2007, 20.81% on pay up to 25,000 SEK a month from 1 April 2026 to 30 September 2027; 31.42% above that (Tax-Parameters-2026).

Example (computed, illustration): a raise of 3,000 SEK a month costs the employer about 3,943 SEK a month in pay plus contributions (3,000 × 1.3142), or about 47,300 SEK a year, before pension and other items.

chunks.heading: How the coach uses this (decision made with the author)
chunks.text:
- Show the employer's cost **as an estimate**, with what is included, when the user asks about budget, or when the employer says cost is the problem (Budget-Is-Fixed, Company-Is-Struggling).
- Use it to build the user's argument: compare the cost with the value the role brings, and with the cost of replacing the user (Employer-Alternative-Cost, RULE-006).
- Use it to find cheaper ways for the employer to give value: non-cash terms often cost the employer less than salary plus contributions (Trade-Across-Issues).
- Never present the employer's cost as the user's concern; it is context for the framing.
- Do not state a contribution rate for a special case (for example pensioners) without checking.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Quoting the employer's cost as 31.42% total, instead of on top of gross.
- Leaving out pension, vacation and insurance costs, which depend on the agreement.
- Using cost as a reason to accept a no.

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: Rates and temporary reductions change. Use Tax-Parameters-2026 and Skatteverket.

Pay in Sweden is quoted as **gross** monthly salary (*bruttolön*). What reaches the account is **net** (*nettolön*): gross minus income tax withheld by the employer. The vault works in **SEK monthly gross**, and the numbers engine converts to yearly, hourly and net amounts (Numbers-Stage).

chunks.heading: How tax is withheld
chunks.text:
- The employer withholds **preliminary tax** at each payment using Skatteverket's tax tables. The user's final tax is settled in the yearly tax return.
- The table depends on the **municipal tax rate** (municipality plus region). The table number follows the rate; check the number for the user's municipality at Skatteverket. Column 1 is used for pay to someone under 66 at the start of the year, whose income gives right to the job tax credit (Tax-Parameters-2026).
- The tables already include the basic allowance and the job tax credit, so the coach does not apply them separately.
- State income tax of 20% is added above the threshold (Income-Tax-Thresholds).
- One-off payments such as a bonus are withheld with a separate table (Tax-on-Benefits-and-Bonus).

chunks.heading: What the numbers engine does (decision made with the author)
chunks.text:
1. Ask for the municipality only if the user wants a net figure (slot `tax_municipality`, tier P3).
2. Use Skatteverket's published tax tables for the user's rate. If the municipality is unknown, use the national average of 32.38% (2026) and label the result a rough estimate.
3. Compute the **marginal effect** of a raise by comparing net at the current gross and at the new gross.
4. Always label net figures `[computed]` and **approximate**. The payslip may differ.
5. The engine specification must record the table source, the year, and the fallback.

chunks.heading: How the coach uses this
chunks.text:
- Keep the negotiation in gross. Show net only on request or when the user compares offers where tax differs (benefits, salary exchange).
- When the user asks "how much more would I get?" show the approximate monthly net for the increase and say it depends on the municipality and total income.
- Never ask for personal identity numbers or bank details (Boundaries-and-Ethics).
- If a raise takes the user above the state tax threshold, say that the part above the threshold is taxed more (Income-Tax-Thresholds).
- For salary exchange and pre-tax benefits, see Salary-Exchange.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Comparing a gross figure with a colleague's or a friend's net figure.
- Using the national average as if it were the user's rate.
- Treating the estimate as the payslip.

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: Tax tables and parameters change every year. Check Tax-Parameters-2026 and Skatteverket.

Swedish earned income is taxed by the municipality (about a third of the income) and, above a threshold, by the state (20% more). This matters in a negotiation because **each extra krona of gross is taxed at the marginal rate**, so a raise is worth less after tax than it looks, and more so above the threshold.

chunks.heading: The main levels (2026, see [[Tax-Parameters-2026]])
chunks.text:
- **Municipal tax:** 32.38% on average (28.93% to 35.65% by municipality).
- **State tax:** 20% on taxable earned income above 643,000 SEK a year. The practical breakpoint is about 660,400 SEK a year of gross earned income (about 55,000 SEK a month) for people under 66.
- **Basic allowance and job tax credit:** reduce tax at lower and middle incomes; the tax tables include them.
- **General pension fee:** 7% up to a cap, offset by a tax reduction of the same size, so it does not reduce net pay in the normal case.

chunks.heading: Marginal tax: what the user keeps
chunks.text:
| Situation | Approximate marginal rate |
|---|---|
| Below the state tax threshold | About the municipal rate (about 32% on average); the job tax credit can move it a little at some income levels |
| Above the state tax threshold | Municipal rate plus 20%: about **52%** on average (32.38% + 20%) |

Example (computed, using the national average rate, for illustration): a raise of 3,000 SEK a month above the threshold leaves about 1,430 SEK after tax (3,000 × (1 − 0.5238)); below the threshold it leaves about 2,030 (3,000 × (1 − 0.3238)). The engine uses the tax tables, not this shortcut (Gross-vs-Net-Pay).

chunks.heading: How the coach uses this
chunks.text:
- When a user compares a raise with a non-cash benefit, say that tax makes the raise worth less than its gross value, and that some benefits are untaxed or taxed differently (Tax-on-Benefits-and-Bonus, Salary-Exchange).
- For a user near the threshold, say that part of the raise is taxed more heavily, and that the marginal rate depends on total income, including other income.
- Do not give tax planning advice. Point to Skatteverket or a tax adviser for individual cases (Boundaries-and-Ethics).
- Pension contributions and some benefits are handled in Occupational-Pension.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Treating the 52% as the user's average tax.
- Ignoring that 2026 figures change each year.
- Using the shortcut where exact table values are available.

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: Thresholds, allowances and credits change each January. Use Tax-Parameters-2026 and Skatteverket.

chunks.heading: One-off payments (bonus)
chunks.text: - With time-based salary, a one-off payment is withheld using the one-off table (*engångstabell*) according to the expected annual income. Without time-based salary, 30% is withheld. The payslip figure is preliminary; see Tax-on-Benefits-and-Bonus.

chunks.heading: Rules for use
chunks.text:
- Every figure shown to the user is tagged `[computed]` or `[researcher]` with this note's date, and is described as an **estimate**.
- If today's date is in a later income year, the coach must say that the figures are for 2026 and that the rates for the new year have not been checked here.
- The temporary reduction ends on 30 September 2027; check before using it for any later date.
- Update procedure: replace each value from Skatteverket's "Belopp och procent" page for the new year, then SCB's municipal rates, then employer contributions; update `valid_as_of` and the changelog.

chunks.heading: Tax table files (Skatteverket, read 2026-11-21)
chunks.text: Skatteverket publishes plain-text (.txt) files for software: monthly tables (`allmanna-tabeller-manad.txt`) and municipal tax rates (`skattesatser-kommuner-2026.txt`), plus a PDF of the monthly tables. The tables are built on combined tax and fee rates of 29 to 42, one table per whole percent; column 1 is for pay to people under 66 at the start of the year. How the municipal file maps to a table number is read from that file when the engine is built (Numbers-Engine-Spec).

chunks.heading: Where these figures are repeated
chunks.text: Other notes quote some of these figures for readability. Update them in the same January pass: Income-Tax-Thresholds (state tax threshold, breakpoint), Employer-Contributions-and-Total-Cost (31.42%, temporary reduction), Company-Car-and-Taxable-Benefits (price base amount), Occupational-Pension (income base amount), and the Numbers-Engine-Spec (employer cost line).

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: Check the Skatteverket page for the current income year before any figure is used in a recommendation.

Bonuses and most benefits are **taxable as employment income**. A bonus or benefit with a stated value is therefore worth less after tax. This note covers how they are taxed and how the coach shows their value.

chunks.heading: Bonus and other one-off payments (checked 2026-11-21)
chunks.text:
- A one-off payment (*engångsbelopp*) is pay for work that is not tied to a set period or paid regularly, such as a bonus, retroactive pay or holiday pay.
- With time-based salary, the employer withholds on the one-off payment with the **one-off table** (*engångstabell*), based on the expected annual income (*årslön*) including the one-off amount. Without time-based salary, **30%** is withheld. Example from Skatteverket's 2026 column 1: an annual income of 100,000 SEK falls in a bracket with 21% withheld.
- The withholding is **preliminary**; the final tax is settled on total income in the tax return. Check the details at Skatteverket.

chunks.heading: How the coach shows a bonus (decision made with the author)
chunks.text: Show the net value of a bonus as the bonus taxed at the user's **marginal rate** (Income-Tax-Thresholds), approximately 32% on average below the state tax threshold and about 52% above, and say that the payslip withholding can differ. Label it `[computed]` and approximate. Do not quote the one-off table percentages as the user's final tax.

chunks.heading: Benefits
chunks.text:
- Discounts, bonuses and similar benefits are **taxable** as income from employment, valued at market value, unless a specific exception applies. A personal discount can be tax-free only if it meets all of Skatteverket's conditions (offered to all staff, not exchangeable for cash, not payment for work, regular range, not unusually large, and not given through a gross salary deduction).
- **Employer loans** at low or zero interest: the benefit is the difference to a comparison rate (the state loan rate at the loan date plus 1.5 percentage points, minimum 0.5%) applied to the loan amount.
- **Car benefit** is valued by a formula based on the price base amount and the new price of the car, plus vehicle tax; see Company-Car-and-Taxable-Benefits.
- **Housing benefit** is valued at local rent.
- Wellness benefits, pension contributions and salary exchange have their own rules (Wellness-Allowance, Occupational-Pension, Salary-Exchange).
- Equity and options are taxed according to their own rules (Employee-Options-and-Equity).

chunks.heading: How the coach shows a taxable benefit (decision made with the author)
chunks.text:
- State the taxable benefit value (as the employer or Skatteverket's valuation gives it) and show an **approximate** after-tax effect at the user's marginal rate, so the benefit can be compared with cash (Total-Comp-Valuation-Rules).
- Do not invent a valuation: use the figure from the offer, the employer or Skatteverket. If it is unknown, say so and ask the employer.
- Mark the result approximate and tell the user to check with the employer or Skatteverket for their own case.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Treating a bonus or a benefit as untaxed.
- Quoting the gross bonus as take-home.
- Valuing equity or a car benefit without the tax treatment.

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: Skatteverket's rules and tables change each year. Check the pages and Tax-Parameters-2026.
When the user's case differs from the source's group (age, experience, education, sector, region), the researcher adjusts **only with data**, never with remembered multipliers.

chunks.heading: Rules
chunks.text:
1. **Use a published breakdown.** SCB's tables give averages by sector, sex, age, education and region for occupations (SCB-Salary-Statistics). If the user's group exists as a breakdown, use that group's figure instead of adjusting.
2. **No invented factors.** A rule of thumb such as "add a given percentage per year of experience" is not used unless a source states it and the researcher cites it.
3. **If no breakdown exists, do not adjust.** Return the unadjusted figure, say which way the user's case probably differs (higher or lower) and lower the confidence.
4. **Do not adjust for gender.** Show a figure for the user's occupation and let the user decide; where the source gives women's pay as a share of men's, report it only if the user asks or the question is pay equity.
5. **Sector and region:** use the breakdown that matches. SCB's cross-tables by region and sector exist; use them rather than a general uplift.
6. **Record every adjustment** in the output (Output-Schema): what, why, source.

chunks.text: That is the coach's job (evidence, Coach-Persona-and-Rules hard rule 8). The researcher does not move the range for it.

Every researched range carries a confidence level in words: **low**, **medium** or **high**, with the reasons. No percentage (D65 applies to data as well as to guesses).

chunks.heading: How the level is set
chunks.text:
Count the points below; the level follows from them. Any one **cap** limits the level whatever the count.

| Factor | Counts towards a higher level when |
|---|---|
| Source tier | At least one tier-1 or tier-2 source (Source-Hierarchy) |
| Fit | Occupation, sector, region and experience match the user's case |
| Range available | A source actually gives quartiles or a range (D68) |
| Agreement | A second independent source agrees (Triangulation-Rules) |
| Recency | Source is within its own publication cycle |
| Size | The source says the group is large; a small group has a wide error |

| Caps | Maximum level |
|---|---|
| Only an average, no range from any source | low |
| Only self-reported or gated sources | low |
| Sources disagree widely | medium |
| Occupation or sector only roughly matched | medium |
| Data older than its next scheduled publication | medium |

**Guide:** three or more factors and no cap is **high**; two factors, or a cap at medium, is **medium**; one or none, or a cap at low, is **low**.

chunks.heading: What the coach says
chunks.text: "Confidence: medium. Reason: two sources agree, but the occupation group is broad." The reason is always given. Low confidence comes with how to firm it up.

chunks.heading: What this is not
chunks.text: It is not a probability that the user's pay will fall in the range, and not a quality score of the user's case.

What the researcher returns to the coach. Plain structured text (JSON or equivalent). Fields marked **required** must be present; if a value is missing, say so in the field rather than leaving it out.

```
request:
  role_description        # required, as received
  normalised_group        # required, name and SSYK code, or "unmapped"
  sector, region, experience_band
unit: "SEK per month, gross, full-time equivalent"   # required
range:                    # required block
  p25: number | null      # only if a source provides it
  median: number | null
  p75: number | null
  average: number | null  # shown when only an average exists
  range_note: text        # e.g. "range unavailable; source gives average only"
confidence:               # required
  level: low | medium | high
  reasons: [text]
sources:                  # required, at least one or an explicit "none found"
  - name, tier, measure (average|median|quartile|advertised range)
    value, year_or_date, retrieved_on, url_or_reference
adjustments_applied: [ {what, why, source} ]
caveats: [text]
valid_as_of: date
user_data: [ {value, note} ]      # tagged [user], shown beside, never merged
gaps_and_next_steps: [text]       # how to firm up the answer
total_comp_facts: [ ... ]         # optional, see Total-Comp-Valuation-Rules
```

chunks.heading: Rules
chunks.text:
- No number without a source entry.
- `confidence.reasons` is never empty.
- If nothing was found: `range` fields are null, `confidence.level` is low, `sources` is "none found", and `gaps_and_next_steps` says what to bring.
- The coach's slot `market_range` is filled from `range`, `confidence` and `valid_as_of` (Slot-Definitions); money values go through the numbers engine (Numbers-Engine-Spec).
The researcher is the part of the system that finds market pay data. It returns facts with sources, never advice. The coach turns the result into advice.

chunks.heading: Steps
chunks.text:
1. **Read the request.** The coach sends role, experience, sector, employer type, location and path. The user's own target is not shared. Missing basics are returned as questions, not guessed.
2. **Normalise the title** to an occupational group (Title-Normalization).
3. **Pick sources** by sector and role from the catalogue (Source-Catalog-Index), in the order of Source-Hierarchy.
4. **Fetch the figures live.** Do not use remembered numbers. Record, for every figure: source, year or date, measure (average, median, quartile or advertised range), unit and basis (monthly gross, full-time).
5. **Put figures on one basis:** SEK per month, gross, full-time equivalent. Keep the original with its unit; note any conversion.
6. **Triangulate** (Triangulation-Rules).
7. **Apply adjustments only where the data supports them** (Adjustment-Factors).
8. **Set the range and confidence** (Confidence-Scoring).
9. **Return the structured result** (Output-Schema), including gaps and the cheapest way to firm up the answer.
10. **Total package, if asked:** return facts and employer-cost estimates for non-cash parts, not a value (Total-Comp-Valuation-Rules).

chunks.heading: Rules
chunks.text:
- **Never invent a figure.** A missing figure is reported as missing.
- **Range method (decision D68):** report P25, median and P75 only where a source actually provides them. If a source gives only an average, return the average, say that no range is available from that source, and set confidence to low unless another source gives a range.
- **Say which measure each figure is.** An average and a median are not interchangeable.
- **Live data only:** every figure carries a retrieval date. Figures older than the source's own publication cycle are flagged.
- **User data counts as user data:** figures from the user are tagged `[user]` and shown beside, not merged into, the researched range.
- **No names:** never return or store the pay of a named person.
- **Stay neutral:** the researcher does not know the user's target.

chunks.heading: When data is thin
chunks.text: Widen nothing silently. Return what exists, set confidence low, name the missing piece, and list what the user can bring: job ads with pay ranges, union statistics, colleagues' experience in general terms.

chunks.heading: Output goes to
chunks.text: The coach, which shows the range with sources, confidence and date (hard rules 2, 3 and 17 in Coach-Persona-and-Rules).
Tier 3 (Source-Hierarchy). Some employers state pay in ads. What the law requires is in Pay-Transparency-Status; do not assert a requirement from here.

chunks.heading: What the Indeed help page says
chunks.text:
- An employer can state pay as an **exact amount**, a **range**, a **starting amount** ("börjar på") or a **maximum** ("upp till").
- If several figures are entered, Indeed shows the first. Pay in points systems must be converted to hourly or monthly pay.
- Formatting errors (missing period or currency, words instead of numbers) can stop pay being displayed.
- The page does not describe how Indeed estimates pay where an employer gives none.

chunks.heading: How the researcher uses it
chunks.text:
- Read the type: a minimum or a "starting amount" is not a range; a maximum is not what is paid.
- Collect several ads for the same occupation, region and level; one ad is an anecdote.
- Report as `advertised range`, with the number of ads and dates; never blend with statistics (Triangulation-Rules).
- Ads state what the employer is prepared to offer new hires, so they are most useful in path A.
- Many Swedish ads state no pay; absence is not data.

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: Platforms change how they show pay; re-check the platform's help page.

Tier 1 (Source-Hierarchy). Pay in municipalities, regions and the state is often set by agreement, so statistics show levels but not the user's own scale (Public-vs-Private-Sector, Collective-Agreements).

chunks.text:

Average monthly salary by occupation, sex, age, region, industry, education and extent of employment; some tables give basic salary, pay dispersion and the share of employees by pay interval. No separate limitations section; the page points to annual quality declarations.
- **Regions and the state:** the page says corresponding statistics exist for the state and private sectors and for regions, but those pages were not read today.
- **Individual public pay:** under the public-access principle some pay information is open (Public-Access-to-Salary-Info).

chunks.heading: How the researcher uses it
chunks.text:
- Report averages; quartiles are not confirmed.
- Ask for the agreement and the pay scale or grade; placement within the scale matters more than the average.
- Say that the statistic describes levels paid, not the user's room to negotiate.

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: Check the latest year and the quality declaration.
Tier 4 (Source-Hierarchy). Recruitment firms publish yearly salary guides.

chunks.heading: Checked today
chunks.text:
One report page (Nigel Wright, Sweden, consumer sector, 2026): it says it covers professionals' salaries in the consumer sector with Nordic workforce insights. It does **not** name roles, say how figures were produced, or say whether they are averages or ranges, and the page appears to be gated behind a form.

Other firms' guides turned up in searches (Michael Page, Hays, Randstad and aggregator sites); none was read, so none is described here.

chunks.heading: How the researcher uses it
chunks.text:
- Use only guides that state their method, year and measure.
- Treat a gated or method-less guide as context, not as a source of the range: confidence capped at low if it is the only source (Confidence-Scoring).
- Never copy a recruiter's number into the range; show it beside the others (Triangulation-Rules).
- Remember that recruiters sell hiring services; ranges may reflect asking offers.

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: Guides are yearly; check the year and the method each time.
Tier 1 (Source-Hierarchy). Official statistics, with Medlingsinstitutet responsible for the wage statistics.

chunks.heading: Lönesök (the search tool)
chunks.text:
- Shows **average** monthly salary before tax for an occupation, as **gross full-time equivalent**, from the wage structure statistics. The page says the statistics were produced in 2024 and does not name a reference year.
- Search by occupation; the page links an SSYK search tool (Title-Normalization).
- Compare by education, sex, age and private or public sector.
- **Medians and percentiles are on separate pages**; the Lönesök page itself shows averages only.
- **Limits stated by SCB:** averages do not account for age distribution, experience, skills or responsibility; the sample is a random sample of companies each year; small occupational groups are more uncertain in a single year.

chunks.heading: Lönestrukturstatistik, hela ekonomin (the database)
chunks.text:
- Tables for **2025**, dated **2026-06-16**; published yearly; **next publication 2027-05-31**.
- Mean basic and monthly pay by occupation (SSYK 2012, 3 and 4 digits), sector, sex, age, education, region and industry; pay dispersion; women's pay as a share of men's; some time series back to 1992.
- **Quartiles by occupation exist (checked 2026-11-22):** table **TAB5932** (`AM0110A/LoneSpridSektYrk4AN`), "Genomsnittlig månadslön och lönespridning efter sektor, yrke (SSYK 2012) och kön", years 2023 to 2025, gives the average, median and the 10th, 25th, 75th and 90th percentiles for about 430 four-digit occupation groups, by sector (all, public, private) and sex, with 95% confidence intervals. Example, group 3312 Banktjänstemän, all sectors, both sexes, 2025: average 47 400, median 43 700, 25th percentile 35 200, 75th percentile 53 100 kr a month.
- The page does not define the pay measure beyond "grund- och månadslön"; whether supplements are included was not stated. Check the annual quality declaration before relying on it.

chunks.heading: Konjunkturlönestatistik (wage growth)
chunks.text: Monthly wage **change**, not levels; published about two months after pay is paid; public sector is a full count, private sector a sample of firms with at least five employees; early figures are usually revised upward later. Use for wage growth context, not for pay levels.

chunks.heading: How the app uses it (D114)
chunks.text: The app reads TAB5932 directly through SCB's open API (PxWebApi): the cheap model picks the occupation group from SCB's own list, then code fetches the figures, so they are exact and no web search is needed. Only an occupation code and a sector are sent to SCB. If SCB has no figures, the web researcher runs instead, once.

chunks.heading: How the researcher uses it
chunks.text:
- Start here for the occupation average; use the age, education, region and sector cross-tables instead of rules of thumb (Adjustment-Factors).
- Report as `average` with `range` unavailable unless a table gives quartiles.
- Confidence is capped at low if SCB is the only source and gives only an average (Confidence-Scoring).

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: Table lists and years change each year; re-check the latest year and the quality declaration.
Tier 2 (Source-Hierarchy). A web-based statistics programme for members of Saco-affiliated unions.

chunks.heading: What the page says (SULF, updated 2026-07-07)
chunks.text:
- Shows average salaries and salary ranges by age group, graduation year, educational programme, labour-market sector and more. Medians and quartiles are not mentioned.
- Data: "various databases containing information from employers and survey data". SCB is not mentioned.
- **Access:** a simple salary calculator based on employer and union statistics is open to everyone; job-specific statistics need membership of a Saco union.
- No data year and no limitations are stated on the page checked.

chunks.heading: How the researcher uses it
chunks.text:
- Use the open calculator when the user has a university degree; ask whether the user is a member and can read their own figures (user data, User-Supplied-Data).
- Do not report member-only figures the researcher cannot see.
- Without a stated year or method, treat as medium fit at most (Confidence-Scoring).

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: Check the year and the scope on the Saco site.
Tier 5 (Source-Hierarchy). Sites where users submit their own pay, or that estimate pay from mixed data.

chunks.heading: What was checked
chunks.text: No salary site's method was verified today. The Indeed help page checked describes how employers enter pay in ads, not how Indeed makes its pay estimates.

chunks.heading: Known limits (general, to be checked per site)
chunks.text:
- Submissions are not verified and the samples are self-selected.
- Pay may be total package, base only or an estimate, and the site may not say.
- Small samples for narrow roles; old entries may linger.

chunks.heading: How the researcher uses it
chunks.text:
- Use only as a cross-check and say so; never as the only basis. Confidence is capped at low when these are the only sources (Confidence-Scoring).
- Record the site, the sample size if given, and the pay definition if given.
- If the site does not say how its figure is built, say that.

chunks.text: Check each site's own method statement before relying on it.

- The member tool draws on data from over 84,000 engineer salaries; full statistics are for members and in Swedish.

chunks.heading: Not checked today
chunks.text: Other unions' statistics (for example Unionen, Naturvetarna, Finansförbundet, Vårdförbundet) appeared in searches but their pages were not read. Do not describe their data until checked. For the user's own union, ask whether it offers salary statistics.

chunks.heading: How the researcher uses it
chunks.text:
- Ask which union the user belongs to and whether they can read the statistics; treat what they report as `[user]` data.
- Public union figures are usually averages by group: report as averages, range unavailable, unless a quartile is shown.
- Union data adds fit (experience, sector) to the SCB average (Triangulation-Rules).

chunks.heading: Verify before use
chunks.text: Method and year differ per union; check each source's own page.
Data the user brings: a pay slip figure, an offer, a union statistic they can read, an ad, general colleague experience.

chunks.heading: Rules
chunks.text:
- Tagged `[user]` and shown **beside** the researched range, never merged into it (Output-Schema).
- If it is credible and comparable, it can raise or lower confidence by confirming or contradicting the researched range (Triangulation-Rules).
- If it is not comparable (different role, region, year, or net instead of gross), say why and ask for the missing detail.
- Never record the pay of a named colleague; ask the user to describe it generally.
- Ask for the figure, not the document. No ID numbers or bank details.
- A single data point is an anecdote and is described as one.

chunks.heading: Why it ranks as it does
chunks.text: It is close to the user's case but is one person's data. It supports the user's argument but does not replace the market range.

Sources are ordered by how well they can be checked and how closely they match the user's case. A higher tier does not always win: a tier-1 figure for the wrong occupation is worse than a tier-3 figure for the right one.

| Tier | Source type | Why it ranks here | Typical limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Official statistics (SCB-Salary-Statistics, Public-Sector-Salary-Lookup) | Random samples or full counts, public methods, annual | Averages, broad occupation groups, a year or more old |
| 2 | Union and Saco statistics (Union-Salary-Statistics, Saco-Salary-Tool) | Large member surveys, often by experience and sector | Members only in part; method often not public |
| 3 | Pay ranges in job ads (Job-Ads-With-Pay-Ranges) | Current and employer-stated | Starting offers or maxima; not what is actually paid |
| 4 | Recruiter salary guides (Recruiter-Salary-Guides) | Current, role-specific | Method rarely stated; often gated; commercial |
| 5 | Self-reported sites (Self-Reported-Salary-Sites) | Large, current | Unverified, skewed samples |
| User | User-Supplied-Data | Closest to the case | One person's data; tagged `[user]`, shown beside, not merged |

chunks.heading: Rules
chunks.text:
- Start from tier 1 and add others to test it, not the reverse.
- Match **before** ranking: occupation, sector, region, experience. Prefer a tier-2 source that fits over a tier-1 that does not.
- Never average across tiers; use Triangulation-Rules.
- Self-reported data alone gives confidence low (Confidence-Scoring).
- Record the tier of every source in the output (Output-Schema).

Job titles vary between employers. Statistics use an occupational classification. SCB's tables use **SSYK 2012** at three and four digits, and its Lönesök page links an SSYK search tool for finding the group.

chunks.heading: Steps
chunks.text:
1. Ask for the **work done**, not only the title: tasks, responsibility, team, tools.
2. Map the description to the occupational group with SCB's SSYK search tool. Record the group and its code in the output.
3. If two groups fit, return both, or the broader one with lower confidence.
4. **Seniority labels** ("senior", "lead", "head of") differ between employers. Do not shift the group because of the word; use experience and responsibility in the description, and the age or education breakdowns where they exist (Adjustment-Factors).
5. **Small groups** carry more uncertainty in a single year (SCB's own caution). Prefer the broader group, and say so.
6. If the role is new or hybrid, use the closest group and name the difference.

chunks.heading: What the coach is told
chunks.text: The normalised title, the code, and any doubt, for example "Mapped to group X; the job also includes Y, so the figure may be low."

chunks.heading: Do not
chunks.text:
- Do not guess a code from memory; look it up each time.
- Do not use a brand-specific title as a group.

**Decision D69:** the researcher returns **facts and the employer's cost**, not a value to the user. The user decides how much each non-cash part matters, with the points comparison (Package-Scoring-Guide). The coach never turns the parts into one total value.

chunks.heading: What is returned for each part
chunks.text:
| Part | Facts returned | Labelled estimate | Source note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base salary | Monthly gross | Net estimate via the engine | Gross-vs-Net-Pay |
| Occupational pension | Agreement and percentage rates | Monthly and yearly SEK for the user's salary | Occupational-Pension |
| Vacation | Days, supplement rule | Supplement per year at the statutory rate | Vacation |
| Variable pay | Scheme, cap, criteria | Range of outcomes, never expected pay | Variable-Pay-and-Bonus |
| Benefits | What and whether taxable | After-tax estimate for taxable ones | Benefits, Company-Car-and-Taxable-Benefits, Wellness-Allowance |
| Insurances | Which apply under the agreement | None (no value) | Insurances |
| Equity | Type, vesting, strike | None (uncertain, shown separately) | Employee-Options-and-Equity |
| Employer cost | Contributions and pension cost | Total employer cost | Employer-Contributions-and-Total-Cost |

chunks.heading: Rules
chunks.text:
- Every SEK figure is tagged `[computed]` or `[assumed]` and labelled as an estimate.
- Parts are listed **beside** base salary and never added into it.
- A part with no verified rate is reported as "unknown, ask the employer".
- The researcher never states a market value for insurance or equity.
- Swedish figures follow the `valid_as_of` and `verify_before_use` flags of the Sweden notes.

How to combine several sources into one range without inventing precision.

1. **Compare like with like.** Convert every figure to monthly gross full-time SEK (Research-Method). Keep the measure: average, median, quartile, advertised minimum or maximum.
2. **Do not mix measures into one number.** An average and a median can be shown side by side; they are never averaged together.
3. **Take the range from sources that give a range.** P25, median and P75 come from a source that publishes them. Where only averages exist, report the average and say the range is unavailable from that source (D68).
4. **Use other sources to test, not to blend.** If a second source's average or range lies inside or near the first, say they agree. If not, show both and the gap.
5. **Weigh by fit and tier** (Source-Hierarchy): occupation match, sector, region, experience, year.
6. **Disagreement is information.** When sources differ by a large margin, widen the stated uncertainty, name the likely reasons (sector mix, experience, year, measure) and set confidence no higher than medium.
7. **Ads show the market's entry point.** A pay range in an ad is what the employer says it will pay for the post; compare it with statistics, do not merge it.
8. **User data** goes beside the result, tagged `[user]`.
9. **Stop at what the data supports.** If two sources do not overlap in occupation or year, return both separately.

The agreement test (do the sources agree?) feeds Confidence-Scoring.

Used when the written terms meet the user's plan after the checks. It confirms the agreed terms point by point so that nothing is left to memory (A-Accepting-and-Confirming-in-Writing). The user sends it only after the contract or offer letter matches what was discussed.

chunks.heading: English
Svenska
Rules
chunks.text:
- List every agreed term, including pension, vacation and notice period if they were discussed.
- Compare the contract with the email before signing; differences go to the employer in writing, and legal questions to a union or lawyer (Boundaries-and-Ethics).
- Do not use the email to open new requests.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Accepting by phone and never confirming terms in writing.
- Leaving out a term that mattered.

Used after an offer, when the user wants to ask for better terms. One request per paragraph, a reason from evidence, one number or package from the approved set, and a date. The walk-away and the target range never appear.

chunks.heading: English
chunks.text:
```
Subject: {{role}} offer: a few points to discuss

Hi {{name}},

Thank you for the offer for the {{role}} position. I'm excited about the role and the team.

I've looked through the package. Based on the market range for this role ({{range}}, {{source}}, {{date}}) and my experience in {{skill}}, I'd like to propose a base salary of {{anchor}} per month.

{{Optional: I would also like to discuss {{other term}}.}}

Could we find 20 minutes this week to talk it through? I'm keen to find a solution that works well for both of us.

Best regards,
{{user name}}
```

chunks.heading: Svenska
chunks.text:
```
Ämne: Erbjudande som {{role}}: några punkter att diskutera

Hej {{name}},

Tack för erbjudandet om tjänsten som {{role}}. Jag är glad över rollen och teamet.

Jag har gått igenom paketet. Utifrån marknadsnivån för rollen ({{range}}, {{source}}, {{date}}) och min erfarenhet av {{skill}} vill jag föreslå en grundlön på {{anchor}} per månad.

{{Valfritt: Jag vill också gärna prata om {{other term}}.}}

Kan vi hitta 20 minuter den här veckan för att prata igenom det? Jag vill gärna hitta en lösning som fungerar bra för oss båda.

Vänliga hälsningar,
{{user name}}
```

chunks.heading: Rules
chunks.text:
- Use only approved figures; the range is shown with its source and date or left out.
- No claim about another offer unless it is real, and then only if the strategy says to mention it (Competing-Offer).
- No threat, no deadline for them, no walk-away.
- If the user has not been given time, send Request-More-Time-Email first.
- Offer the spoken version too if the channel is unknown.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Several numbers in one email.
- An angry or long email; stay below about 150 words.
- Sending before the total package has been checked (A-Offer-Analysis).
Declining politely and clearly keeps the door open (A-Declining-Gracefully). Short, warm, no long reasons, no negotiation left open by accident.

chunks.heading: English
chunks.text:
```
Subject: Re: {{role}} offer

Hi {{name}},

Thank you for the offer and for the time you and the team have spent with me. After careful consideration I've decided not to accept the position.

{{Optional, one sentence: This was a difficult decision; I was impressed by {{specific thing}}.}}

I appreciate the process and wish you and the team all the best. I hope our paths cross again.

Best regards,
{{user name}}
```

chunks.heading: Svenska
Rules
chunks.text:
- Say no clearly in the first paragraph; do not leave a half-open door unless the user means it.
- Give no more reason than the user wants to; never an untrue one.
- Do not criticise the employer or the pay.
- If the user wants to leave room for a better offer, use Counter-Offer-Email instead.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Declining by silence.
- Writing "unfortunately the salary was too low" when the user would rather keep the relationship; say it only if it is the user's choice.
Sent the same day, it puts what was said and agreed on record and sets the next step and date (B-Follow-Up-Plan). It also works after path A meetings. Written neutrally, even when the answer was no.

chunks.heading: English
Svenska
Rules
chunks.text:
- Write only what was actually said or agreed.
- Always include a date for the next step.
- After a no: thank them, keep the next step (dated review with criteria), do not argue again.
- For path A confirmation of terms use Accept-and-Confirm-Email.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Waiting days to write.
- Adding new demands in a summary email.
A short, polite email asking for a dated pause before answering an offer (Ask-for-Time). Send it the same day the offer arrives.

chunks.heading: English
chunks.text:
```
Subject: Re: {{role}} offer

Hi {{name}},

Thank you again for the offer. I'm very interested and want to give you a considered answer.

Could I come back to you by {{date}}? I'd like to go through the full package properly. If it helps, I can send two questions in writing today.

Best regards,
{{user name}}
```

chunks.heading: Svenska
chunks.text:
```
Ämne: Re: Erbjudande som {{role}}

Hej {{name}},

Tack igen för erbjudandet. Jag är mycket intresserad och vill ge dig ett genomtänkt svar.

Kan jag återkomma senast {{date}}? Jag vill gå igenom hela paketet ordentligt. Om det underlättar kan jag skicka två frågor skriftligt i dag.

Vänliga hälsningar,
{{user name}}
```

chunks.heading: Rules
chunks.text:
- A real date, within a few working days. Do not give a reason that is untrue.
- If they set a short deadline, ask once whether it can move (Exploding-Deadline) and keep the date you give.
- Attach nothing and promise nothing else.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- No date.
- Asking for so long that the employer moves on.
Used on path B to book a conversation about pay, preferably **before budgets are set** (B-Timing-and-Budget-Cycle). It is short, businesslike and gives the manager time to prepare.

chunks.heading: English
chunks.text:
```
Subject: Booking time to talk about my salary

Hi {{name}},

I'd like to book {{30 minutes}} to talk about my salary and my role going forward. {{Optional: Since {{date}} my responsibilities have grown to include {{scope}}.}}

Would {{day/time options}} work? If it helps, I can send a short summary of my results in advance.

Best regards,
{{user name}}
```

chunks.text:
```
Ämne: Boka tid för att prata om min lön

Hej {{name}},

Jag vill gärna boka {{30 minuter}} för att prata om min lön och min roll framöver. {{Valfritt: Sedan {{date}} har mitt ansvar vuxit till att omfatta {{scope}}.}}
```
