| Rules illustrated | RULE-040, RULE-039 (see Decision-Rules) |

chunks.heading: Lessons for the salary chatbot
chunks.text:
- In a raise conversation, **one concrete story** of impact ("I took over the X account and cut processing time from five days to two") carries more weight than a general claim (Story-vs-Statistics, B-Evidence-Builder).
- Frame the ask around **what the employer gains or risks losing** (Persuasion-and-Framing).

A purchasing negotiation from Week 4 with several issues: price, quantity, quality guarantee and advertising (branding). This note relies on the Knight Engines role sheet, the class debrief and the class outcome sheet.

> **Whose information is this?** This summary rests on one role sheet and the course debrief. The counterpart's confidential instructions were not available; anything about the other side comes from the debrief slides.

chunks.heading: Situation (paraphrased from Knight's role)
chunks.text:
- The government wants 1,000 V-16Z engines within **60 days**. Knight can build the engines but lacks the **8,000 Class A pistons** needed; they must arrive within **two weeks**.
- Only **Excalibur** can supply on that timescale, on two conditions: its brand is shown on every engine, and a **5% rush mark-up**.
- Manufacturing expects 3–4% defective pistons, so Knight needs a **quality guarantee**, ideally extra pistons with unused ones taken back.
- Price: Class C pistons sell for $250; Knight estimates Class A at about **$500**; the **maximum is $600** to stay competitive in the bid.
- Branding: colleagues think Excalibur should give a discount for the advertising, but the president wants a good relationship because Knight may one day **acquire Excalibur**.
- Knight's alternative: Mordred Technologies at **$470 in four weeks**, too late for the government contract but usable for upgrades.
- Knight is judged on the average price and the quality guarantee.

chunks.heading: The class analysis (Week 4 slides)
chunks.text:
| | Knight | Excalibur (from the debrief) |
|---|---|---|
| Interests | Win the government contract at low cost within two weeks; reputation; possible future acquisition | Sell a surplus of 10,000 pistons above the $480 production cost; marketing; access to government work |
| BATNA | No contract this time; Mordred at $470 in four weeks | Another buyer at about $100 per unit, uncertain future |
| Example price RP / TP | $600 / about $500 | n/a / about $600 including rush and quality fees |

The slides then ask which issues each side prioritises and how to use that: Knight cares most about price, timing and the guarantee; Excalibur values branding and the rush fee. A sample exchange traded a lower price for accepting branding and the fee structure.

chunks.heading: Class results (anonymised)
chunks.text:
- 13 pairs, all reached a deal. Prices ranged from **$470 to $640** (median **$590**). Two deals went above Knight's $600 maximum.
- Almost every deal allowed branding (Excalibur's priority) and most waived the rush fee, so the trade of **branding for price** was widely found.
- Several deals added long-term or exclusive supply agreements, and the lowest price ($470) came with a multi-year contract: **future business was traded for today's price**.

chunks.heading: Case summary (internal)
chunks.text:
Internal summary for the coach and the roleplay simulator. Never shown or cited to the user.

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Situation | Rush purchase of 8,000 pistons in two weeks for a government contract |
| Actors | Knight Engines (buyer); Excalibur Engine Parts (seller) |
| Known information | Knight: market estimate $500, maximum $600, alternative $470 in four weeks (too late) |
| Unknown information | Excalibur's surplus stock and low production cost; how much it wanted government exposure |
| BATNAs | Knight: no government contract this time; Excalibur: a much lower-value sale elsewhere |
| Offers | Excalibur's starting terms: 5% rush fee plus branding |
| Outcome | Prices $470–$640 (median $590); most deals waived the rush fee and allowed branding |
| What worked / failed | Worked: removing the fee and getting the guarantee. Common failure: accepting a price at the buyer's maximum without trading the issues the seller values |
| Focus | Excalibur's interest in branding and government work: trade it for price, not only for fees |
| Do not disclose | The $600 ceiling; the two-week deadline pressure |
| Do disclose | That branding and a future relationship have value to Excalibur |
| Rules illustrated | RULE-024, RULE-048 (see Decision-Rules) |

chunks.heading: Lessons for the salary chatbot
chunks.text:
1. **List every issue** and decide, before the meeting, which ones you care about most (Issue-Prioritisation).
2. **Do not give away an issue for free** that the other side values (here branding; in salary perhaps a start date or flexibility) (Logrolling).
3. **Negotiate the package, not issue by issue** (Package-Deals).
4. A **time-critical need** (Knight's two-week deadline) is a weakness to protect, like a user who must accept quickly.

A dispute from Week 11 between a property developer (**Pat Tan, Meridian Investments**) and a carpentry subcontractor (**Sandy Lim, TimberWorks**). Three linked issues must be settled in one meeting: a disputed invoice, a $200,000 loan and unpaid rent. The outcome comes from the class outcome sheet.

> **Whose information is this?** This summary rests on one role sheet and the course debrief. The counterpart's confidential instructions were not available; anything about the other side comes from the debrief slides.

chunks.heading: Situation (paraphrased from Pat's role; all figures SGD, exercise assumptions)
chunks.text:
- **Relationship:** Meridian is Sandy's lender, landlord and an important customer; nine years without serious problems.
- **Loan:** $200,000 lent five years ago, renewed yearly, interest always paid, principal never repaid. It falls due in 30 days. Pat wants the principal back for a time-limited property opportunity.
- **Lease:** Sandy gave proper notice on a $5,000-a-month workshop, but **$10,000** (two months) is unpaid for no known reason. A new tenant at $6,000 a month is lined up but not yet signed.
- **Invoice:** Pat sold the whole condominium project at a fixed, non-renegotiable price that left about **$250,000 profit**. While Pat was away, Sandy upgraded to **oak** after telling Pat's secretary it would cost "less than three percent". Pat assumed about $200 a unit; Sandy's new invoice is **$950,000 instead of $700,000** ($2,500 more per unit). The painter also asks for $300 more per unit for finishing oak. Together these would turn the profit into a loss.
- **Authority:** the secretary could handle routine details within budget and was told not to approve changes costing money.
- **Contract:** overruns are TimberWorks' responsibility; amendments must be in writing and signed by both.
- **Legal advice:** Pat's position on $700,000 is strong, but deducting the loan and rent from the payment could push Sandy into insolvency, and a trustee could reclaim it as an improper preference.
- **Cash:** Pat needs about $720,000 for committed investments and working capital; available resources total about $730,000 only if Sandy repays the loan and the rent.
- **Emotions:** a hostile phone call with exchanged insults; suspicion that Sandy upgraded to raise her own profit. Pat's family reasons for the trip are private and were not shared.

chunks.heading: Course debrief (Week 11)
chunks.text:
- Disputes differ from deals: there is a past and a rejected claim; BATNAs are **linked**; both sides are in the **domain of loss**; emotions run high; each sees the other negatively.
- Triggers here: miscommunication (the three percent), unforeseen events (Pat's sale), unintended consequences (the painting cost), and distorted attributions (Pat thinks Sandy upgraded for profit; Sandy thinks she did it to help Pat).
- **Interests, rights and power** as three approaches; linked alternatives do not mean equal power, and strong rights do not guarantee recovery (Interests-Rights-Power).
- How to bring a rights- or power-based counterpart back to interests: do not reciprocate contention, stay calm and ask questions, acknowledge without agreeing, take a break, comment on the process, and do not reward obstinacy with concessions (Disputes-and-Emotions).
- The debrief also showed that integrative solutions depended on both sides' cash positions: Sandy's side involved a decision about her house, which Pat's role sheet did not show.

chunks.heading: Class results (anonymised)
chunks.text:
- 11 pairs: 10 agreements and 1 impasse. Invoice payments ranged from **$700k to $920k** (median about $805k).
- Loans were mostly repaid later (3 to 36 months), sometimes with interest of 9–20%. Back rent was usually repaid over time or on a cheque clearing.
- Most Pats kept the hotel and dropped the waterfront property; Sandy sold the house in about half the agreements.
- The pattern: almost nobody held the legal position of $700k and an immediate loan call. The **linked BATNAs** (Sandy's possible insolvency) pushed most pairs toward paying more and waiting longer.

chunks.heading: Case summary (internal)
chunks.text:
Internal summary for the coach and the roleplay simulator. Never shown or cited to the user.

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Situation | Dispute over a $250k invoice increase, linked to a $200k loan and $10k unpaid rent |
| Actors | Pat Tan (developer, lender, landlord); Sandy Lim (carpentry subcontractor) |
| Known information | Contract terms, cash needs (about $720k), the misunderstanding with the secretary |
| Unknown information | Sandy's cash position, her house, her reasons for the upgrade and withheld rent |
| BATNAs | Pat: pay $700k, call the loan, demand rent (legally strong, commercially risky). Linked to Sandy's insolvency risk |
| Offers | Packages combining the invoice, the loan timing and the rent |
| Outcome | Invoice $700k–$920k (median about $805k); loans repaid in 3–36 months; most developers kept the hotel and dropped the waterfront property |
| What worked / failed | Worked: reaching agreement and keeping the relationship. Common failure: moving well beyond the funding ceiling because the BATNAs were linked |
| Focus | Both sides' cash flows; interests over rights; checking every concession against the funding plan |
| Do not disclose | The family reasons behind the trip (private); the exact funding ceiling |
| Do disclose | The fixed sale price and thin margin, which explain why the upgrade gave Pat no benefit |
| Rules illustrated | RULE-041, RULE-042, RULE-009, RULE-048, RULE-036 (see Decision-Rules) |

chunks.heading: Lessons for the salary chatbot
chunks.text:
1. **When a salary talk turns into a dispute** (a broken promise, a missed review), separate interests, rights and power, and lead with interests (B-When-the-Answer-Is-No).
2. **Check authority** before relying on what an intermediary said (Ratification-and-Authority).
3. **Get changes in writing**, signed by the person with authority (A-Accepting-and-Confirming-in-Writing).
4. **Bundle linked issues** into one package so that each side can see the whole (Package-Deals).
5. **Attribution errors** are common: assume a misunderstanding before assuming bad faith (Biased-Perceptions).

A single-issue, cash-only sale of a parking and loading space between two neighbouring business owners, from Week 2. It is the course's main example of **first offers, anchoring and concessions**.

> **Whose information is this?** This summary rests on one role sheet and the course debrief. The counterpart's confidential instructions were not available; anything about the other side comes from the debrief slides.

chunks.heading: Situation
chunks.text:
From the seller's role sheet and the debrief slides:

- Park is closing or relocating the current shop and no longer needs the space, which adds **urgency to sell**.
- Fifteen years earlier, the neighbour (Tan) had **rejected an offer to buy 50% of the space for $10,000**. Such history can make a seller feel weaker than the facts justify.
- Park's **reservation price: $15,000**.
- Debrief: the ZOPA ran from **$15,000 (seller's reservation price) to $40,000 (buyer's)**. The space was worth about **$40,000 in operational efficiency** to Tan, whose current delivery arrangements were costly.
- The debrief also mentioned that Park had another offer, and asked whether and when to reveal it.

chunks.heading: Course debrief (Week 2)
chunks.text:
- Manage information asymmetry: plan what to learn, what to reveal and when, and how to answer "why are you selling?" (Information-Asymmetry).
- Shape perceptions: aggressive but justified anchors, strategic ambiguity about the reason for selling, signalling a BATNA without details, and guarding facts such as the buyer's efficiency gain (Shaping-Perceptions).
- The line between **lying** and **strategic ambiguity**: "another tenant offered $30,000" (a false fact) versus "I have had several inquiries and a firm written offer, but I would prefer to sell to you" (true, if it is true).

chunks.heading: Class results (anonymised)
chunks.text:
- 11 pairs, all reached a deal. Sale prices ranged from **$15.5k to $35k** (median **$28k**).
- The buyer's reservation price was $40k, so even the best seller left value on the table.
- Same case, same information: the spread of almost $20k came from **first offers, justification and concession patterns**, not from facts.

chunks.heading: Case summary (internal)
chunks.text:
Internal summary for the coach and the roleplay simulator. Never shown or cited to the user.

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Situation | Single-issue, cash-only sale of a parking and loading space between neighbours |
| Actors | Park (seller); Tan (buyer) |
| Known information | Seller: RP $15k, urgency (relocating), an old rejected offer of $10k for half the space |
| Unknown information | Buyer's RP ($40k) and the space's efficiency value to the buyer |
| BATNAs | Seller: another offer; buyer: a delivery alternative further away |
| Offers | Seller openings varied; a low, vaguely justified opening ($25k against a $40k value) was met with a counter near $12k |
| Outcome | Sale prices $15.5k–$35k (median $28k) |
| What worked / failed | Failed: low, weakly justified anchor; large concession steps; focusing on the buyer's arguments |
| Focus | The buyer's value from the space; an ambitious, justified anchor; small, shrinking concessions |
| Do not disclose | Urgency to sell; the reservation price |
| Do disclose | That an alternative exists, without details; the space's benefits to the buyer |
| Rules illustrated | RULE-033, RULE-053, RULE-020, RULE-012, RULE-013, RULE-011, RULE-015, RULE-016 (see Decision-Rules) |

chunks.heading: Lessons for the salary chatbot
chunks.text:
1. **Value yourself from the buyer's side.** The employer's value from the hire, not the user's weakest fact, should set the anchor (Make-a-Justified-First-Offer).
2. **A low first number reveals a low reservation price** (Anchoring, First-Offer-Decision).
3. **A weak-feeling position is often weaker in the user's head than in reality**: old history (like a past rejection or a past salary) may not reflect today's value (Weak-Position).
4. **Concede in shrinking steps**, and watch whether the other side is reciprocating (Concession-Strategy).

The course's job-offer negotiation, played online in Week 5 and debriefed in Week 6. A hiring manager (Riley) and a graduating candidate (Hayden) negotiate a first job: salary, start date, relocation and other terms. **This is the case closest to the chatbot's path A**, and the Week 6 debrief covers both roles.

> **Whose information is this?** This summary rests on one role sheet and the course debrief. The counterpart's confidential instructions were not available; anything about the other side comes from the debrief slides.

chunks.heading: Situation (paraphrased from Riley's role)
chunks.text:
- Riley is group product manager at a multimedia software company in New York and has struggled to fill a marketing-analyst role in a new team for teen social-media products.
- Hayden, about to graduate, impressed Riley: initiative, strong grades, some PR experience at a TV station, a personality that fits. Riley's concerns: lack of **industry knowledge** and whether Hayden will **relocate**.
- Pay: the company is not known for top salaries but has a **5–10% bonus** plan and a **6-week sabbatical** every three years. An industry consortium guides starting pay: **$43k–$49k** for a less experienced analyst, **$50k–$56k** for a more experienced one. Riley thinks Hayden belongs in the lower range. No formal relocation policy; the last comparable move was reimbursed about **$1,500**.
- Riley's hidden pressure: a **6-week sabbatical from late June**. Hayden mentioned a European trip around then.
- Riley's BATNA: an experienced alternative candidate who can start **1 June** but insists on **$56k** and seems a poor fit.
- A hire/no-hire decision, including terms, must be made in the meeting.

chunks.heading: Hayden's side (from the Week 6 debrief; not part of Riley's role sheet)
chunks.text:
- Hayden's ranking: (1) New York and this job, which is a near-perfect fit and close to a partner starting graduate study there; (2) a **1 September** start, because a three-month trip from 22 May is booked with non-refundable tickets; (3) salary, with a BATNA of **$60k plus stock** in San Francisco, a location Hayden dislikes; (4) about **$5k relocation, needed up front** because cash is tight.
- The case deliberately does not say how far below $60k Hayden should go.

chunks.heading: Course debrief (Week 6)
chunks.text:
- Riley should compare every concession to the BATNA (an experienced June 1 hire at $56k whom Riley likes less) and use salary within the bands, bonus and relocation to "buy" an early start.
- Hayden should make 1 September something Riley must pay for, use the $60k + stock offer as a credible BATNA, and avoid revealing too soon how much New York matters.
- Effective negotiators were firm but flexible, negotiated the whole package, justified ambitious positions, used anchors and BATNA signals credibly, and listened. Less effective: rigidity, positions before interests, one-issue bargaining, information leakage and implausible anchors (Ask-Anchor-Trade-Adapt).
- One notable agreement in the class: $45k start, 15 May start with remote work to 1 September, a six-month review and a 5–10% bonus after a year.

chunks.heading: Class results (anonymised)
chunks.text:
From the Week 6 results table (names removed):

- 11 pairs reported deals. Starting salaries ranged from **$45k to $57k** (median **$48k**).
- Common extras: relocation support ($2k–$7.5k or a studio flat), performance bonuses, dated reviews with set increases, remote work until the trip ended, signing bonuses and training budgets.
- The variety shows how many issues a "salary" negotiation really contains.

chunks.heading: Case summary (internal)
chunks.text:
Internal summary for the coach and the roleplay simulator. Never shown or cited to the user.

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Situation | First-job offer in New York; start date and relocation in conflict with the candidate's trip |
| Actors | Riley (hiring manager); Hayden (graduating candidate) |
| Known information | Riley: salary bands, bonus, sabbatical, $56k alternative candidate, start-date pressure |
| Unknown information | Hayden's $60k + stock offer, non-refundable trip, need for cash up front, how much New York mattered |
| BATNAs | Riley: experienced candidate at $56k from 1 June; Hayden: $60k + stock in San Francisco |
| Offers | Far apart: a benchmark-based low offer (about $43k plus bonus and sabbatical) against a demand of about $76.5k plus stock and relocation |
| Outcome | Starting salaries $45k–$57k (median $48k); common extras: relocation support, bonuses, dated reviews, remote work until the trip ended |
| What worked / failed | Worked: asking what matters most; redefining the start date. Common failures: defending the benchmark after new information; one-issue bargaining |
| Focus | Interests behind June vs September and behind the salary demand |
| Do not disclose | Riley: the sabbatical deadline. Hayden: how much New York matters |
| Do disclose | Riley: wanting the team running soon. Hayden: the trip constraint and the cash need |
| Rules illustrated | RULE-045, RULE-046, RULE-047, RULE-032, RULE-049, RULE-012, RULE-013 (see Decision-Rules) |

chunks.heading: Lessons for the salary chatbot (the user is usually Hayden)
chunks.text:
1. **Ask what problem a date or a number solves** for the employer before arguing about it (Positions-vs-Interests).
2. **Redefine issues:** remote start, an advance on salary to cover moving, a dated review with criteria (Relocation-or-Remote, Propose-a-Dated-Review).
3. **Know the employer's band and benchmark**, and expect a first offer at the bottom of it for a graduate (First-Job-or-Graduate).
4. **A credible competing offer** moves the employer, if used honestly (Competing-Offer).
5. **Trade, do not just concede:** "If I start remotely in June, can we look at the base?" (Trade-Across-Issues).
6. **Expect the anchor to be challenged:** In one run, a demand of $76.5k against a $60k BATNA and a $43k–$56k band was far outside the range, and the gap took a long time to close (Anchoring).

A three-party negotiation from Week 12 between the owners of three apartments in an old building: the Tans (first floor), Brian Lim (second floor) and the Chens (top floor). The issues are the roof, how its cost is shared, the Chens' private rooftop deck, and Brian's long renovation. The outcome comes from the class outcome sheet.

> **Whose information is this?** This summary rests on one role sheet and the course debrief. The counterpart's confidential instructions were not available; anything about the other side comes from the debrief slides.

chunks.heading: Situation (paraphrased from the Tans' role; figures in SGD)
chunks.text:
- The Tans have lived there 20 years and are saving so their three children can finish university without loans. They will pay for essential shared work but not every improvement.
- **Brian's renovation:** two years of dust and noise, power cut nine times without warning, a cracked ceiling and a ruined chandelier, at least **S$3,000** in repairs. The Tans worry about structural safety and possible missing permits; Brian reacted quickly when they mentioned an official inspection.
- **Decision rules as the Tans understood them:** traditionally unanimous; the Tans believed they could not be made to pay for something they had not approved, but had not read the written by-laws for years.
- **The roof:** the Chens proposed a **S$10,000** replacement; their inspector and several roofers say it is needed. The Tans' own roofer quoted **S$2,550** to patch and silvercoat, lasting about three years (S$850 each). The Chens want their deck for June gatherings; the Tans had suggested work in October or November.
- **The Tans' priorities:** (1) responsible management of Brian's renovation (permits, supervision, notice, completion date, S$3,000 compensation); (2) financial protection and precedent (pay no more than S$850; others split the extra S$7,450 if they insist); (3) the roofing method. Lasting neighbour relations matter, but not at the cost of financial stability. A roof decision must be reached in the meeting.

chunks.heading: Course debrief (Week 12): what the Tans did not know
chunks.text:
- **Different priorities:** the Chens put roof and deck before June first; Brian would pay no more than one-third and wanted to avoid inspection and delay; the Tans put renovation management first.
- **Biased perceptions** on all sides: the Tans saw the roof as "only about their deck", although several experts recommended replacement within a year even without a deck; the Chens assumed Brian's wealth meant willingness to pay; Brian attributed the Tans' resistance to character rather than real constraints.
- **Facts that changed the picture:** the written rules allowed a **two-thirds vote** for spending up to S$25,000, so the Tans had no veto; Brian admitted missing approvals; any extra over about S$1,500 would delay the Chens' deck by a year.
- **Common interests:** better management of Brian's work, good neighbour relations, and shared responsibility for necessary repairs. The real disagreement was which improvements are necessary.
- **Alliances change by issue:** Chens and Brian on replacement and equal sharing; Chens and Tans on safe renovation; Brian and Tans on resolving the damage.
- Next time: map parties and interests, check your own assumptions, build coalitions deliberately, agree process rules, and design agreements with contingencies and monitoring.

chunks.heading: Class results (anonymised)
chunks.text:
- 6 groups, all agreed. **Every group chose immediate full replacement and no inspector.**
- The Tans paid between **S$333 and S$1,833** (the highest share partly deferred). Brian paid the largest share in every group (S$4,833–S$6,333), often linked to the damage.
- Common additions: written agreements on future cost-sharing and renovations, and contingent payments if Brian was found liable.

chunks.heading: Case summary (internal)
chunks.text:
Internal summary for the coach and the roleplay simulator. Never shown or cited to the user.

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Situation | Three neighbours decide on a roof, cost sharing, a private deck and a disruptive renovation |
| Actors | The Tans; Brian Lim; the Chens |
| Known information | Tans: tight finances, damage costs, a S$2,550 patch quote; belief in unanimity |
| Unknown information | Two-thirds voting rule; expert advice for replacement; Brian's missing approvals; the Chens' S$1,500 limit |
| BATNAs | Tans: request an official inspection; vote against (weaker than believed) |
| Offers | Patch at S$850 each vs replacement split three ways |
| Outcome | All six groups chose replacement; the Tans paid S$333–S$1,833; common terms: contingency on damage, notice of renovations |
| What worked / failed | Worked: contingencies and deferral. Common failure: preparation relied on a veto that did not exist |
| Focus | Checking the rules; coalitions per issue; the others' constraints |
| Do not disclose | Exactly how far the Tans could stretch |
| Do disclose | University costs as the real constraint; the priority on safe, supervised renovation |
| Rules illustrated | RULE-036, RULE-043 (see Decision-Rules) |

chunks.heading: Lessons for the salary chatbot
chunks.text:
1. **Check the rules before relying on a veto.** The Tans' belief in unanimity was wrong; a user's belief about the pay system (fixed scale, review cycle) may be too (Fixed-Scale-or-Agreement).
2. **Your necessity is not their necessity:** test self-serving definitions (Biased-Perceptions).
3. **Solve their problem to solve yours** (Solving-the-Other-Sides-Problem).
4. **Several decision makers** (manager, HR, finance) can form different alliances on different issues (Coalitions-and-Multiparty).
The Week 1 exercise. A SingOil representative wants to buy a petrol station from its owner. This note is based on the debrief slides and the class outcome sheet; no role sheet is in the vault.

chunks.heading: Interests (from the debrief)
chunks.text:
| SingOil representative | Station owner |
|---|---|
| A five-year plan; minimise spending on the new station; find an experienced manager; a quick transition to profit (construction, renovation, keeping customers) | A lifelong dream; money for a boat trip; financial security on return; leaving a depressing living situation soon |

chunks.heading: Positions and the reframed deal
chunks.text: On price alone, the slides show **no ZOPA**: the owner's lowest acceptable price is above SingOil's highest. Reframing changes this: SingOil needs an **experienced manager**, and the owner needs **security after the trip**. Adding a job offer as station manager on the owner's return (shown in the slides as worth about $75,000) turns a negative ZOPA into a positive one.

chunks.heading: Preparation categories introduced in Week 1
chunks.text:
- **Self:** BATNA (objective reality), reservation point (worse than this, walk away), target (optimistic; the first offer should be better than this), issues.
- **Other:** BATNA, interests and positions, rapport.
- **Situation:** power differential, type of resource, time pressure.

chunks.heading: Class results (anonymised)
chunks.text:
- 7 of 8 pairs reached a deal. Sale prices ranged from **400K to 450K** (median 435K).
- Almost every deal added a **second issue** for the owner: a guaranteed job or management role on return (75K–125K a year), a consulting share of profits, or contingent pay tied to station revenue. One deal bought 80% of the station for 450K.
- The pattern: price alone rarely closed the gap; **adding the owner's future income** did.

chunks.heading: Case summary (internal)
chunks.text:
Internal summary for the coach and the roleplay simulator. Never shown or cited to the user.

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Situation | A buyer wants a petrol station; the owner wants money for a long boat trip and security afterwards |
| Actors | SingOil representative (buyer); station owner (seller) |
| Known information | Each side's own interests and limits; on price alone the ranges did not overlap |
| Unknown information | The other side's limit; that SingOil needed an experienced manager and the owner needed income on return |
| BATNAs | Buyer: other sites; owner: keep the station or sell to someone else |
| Offers | Price-only offers failed; reframed offers added a job on return |
| Outcome | 7 of 8 pairs agreed at 400K–450K, most with a future role or income for the owner; one impasse |
| What worked / failed | Worked: adding the owner's post-trip income. Failed: treating it as a single price issue |
| Focus | Interests behind the price: SingOil's manager need, the owner's security |
| Do not disclose | Your own reservation price |
| Do disclose | Interests (a manager is needed; security after the trip is needed) so the other side can solve them |
| Rules illustrated | RULE-032, RULE-049, RULE-031 (see Decision-Rules) |

chunks.heading: Lessons for the salary chatbot
chunks.text: - When the numbers do not meet, **look at interests**: what else could make the deal work? For a user, a role change, a dated review or a different start could create a ZOPA (Positions-vs-Interests, Differences-as-Opportunities).

A Week 3 exercise: an L&D manager at Meridian Services buys 500 learning passes for a pilot from SkillSpring's Director of Sales. This note is based on the debrief slides, and the class outcome sheet.

chunks.heading: Key facts (from the debrief)
chunks.text:
- **Buyer's reference points:** SkillSpring's average price $18 a pass ($9,000); LearnPro $16.80 ($8,400) with fewer tracks; QuickLearn $15 ($7,500), basic; larger clients often get discounts; a successful pilot could lead to a bigger contract.
- **Seller's reference points:** small-order price $19.80 ($9,900); average $18; competitor average $16.80; the largest client's maximum 20% discount at $14.40 ($7,200).
- **BATNAs:** buyer, LearnPro at $8,400; seller, keep selling to others and protect its pricing structure.
- **The challenge:** the buyer had to justify paying above its BATNA; the seller had to justify a discount on a small order. Few questions were asked in class.

chunks.heading: What the debrief teaches
chunks.text:
- **Questions address information asymmetry.** Each side had a list of things to find out (why this provider, which features matter, how realistic a larger contract is, what drives discounts, what else can be offered).
- **Options are not side deals:** extra passes, extended pilot, analytics, reference-client status, faster renewal, future volume commitments.
- **Alternative versus option** (Alternative-vs-Option).
- **Share interests and priorities, protect the BATNA** (Questions-You-May-Not-Wish-to-Answer).
- **Objective, independent standards** are credible justifications; budget or affordability reasons are weaker (Reference-Points).

chunks.heading: Class results (anonymised)
chunks.text:
- 13 pairs; 10 deals and **3 no-deals**. Prices ranged from **SGD 15.40 to 25.00** per pass (median 17.40).
- Most deals added a **future-contract** element (volume, multi-year price, referral-based discounts), showing the value of linking today's price to tomorrow's business.

chunks.heading: Case summary (internal)
chunks.text:
Internal summary for the coach and the roleplay simulator. Never shown or cited to the user.

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Situation | A buyer purchases 500 learning passes for a pilot; a possible larger contract next year |
| Actors | Meridian L&D manager (buyer); SkillSpring Director of Sales (seller) |
| Known information | Reference prices: SkillSpring average 18, competitor 16.80, basic option 15 |
| Unknown information | How much the seller valued a new corporate client and future volume; how discounts are set |
| BATNAs | Buyer: competitor at 16.80; seller: keep its price structure with other clients |
| Offers | Buyer: an ambitious opening justified by reference prices (competitor 16.80, basic option 15) |
| Outcome | SGD 15.40–25.00 per pass (median 17.40); 3 no-deals; most deals linked today's price to future business |
| What worked / failed | Worked: ambitious, justified anchor; linking price to future business |
| Focus | Independent reference points; the value of future volume to the seller |
| Do not disclose | Preference for SkillSpring over the competitor; reservation price |
| Do disclose | Interests: a successful pilot, possible referrals and future volume |
| Rules illustrated | RULE-034, RULE-019, RULE-018 (see Decision-Rules) |

chunks.heading: Lessons for the salary chatbot
chunks.text:
- Justify a salary ask with **independent standards** (market statistics, pay band, collective agreement), not personal costs (Use-Market-Data).
- Plan the **questions** for the employer before the meeting (Ask-Diagnostic-Questions).
A team exercise from Week 7 based on the **prisoner's dilemma**. Two neighbouring bubble-tea stalls decide each round whether to **keep** or **cut** prices.

chunks.heading: The game (Week 7 slides)
chunks.text:
Weekly profit in SGD (your profit / their profit):

| | Other stall keeps | Other stall cuts |
|---|---|---|
| **You keep** | 1,200 / 1,200 | 400 / 1,600 |
| **You cut** | 1,600 / 400 | 800 / 800 |

Cutting pays more in any single round, but if both cut, each earns less than if both keep. **Winning the comparison is not the same as doing well.** Communication was allowed only at certain points, and the number of remaining rounds became known near the end.

chunks.heading: Course take-aways (Week 7)
chunks.text:
- Manage the **pattern**, not only the next move. Every move is information that shapes the response.
- A protective move can look like aggression from the other side.
- Cooperation is easier when today's behaviour has tomorrow's consequences; the visible ending removes that.
- For negotiation: use **small reciprocal steps** before accepting large vulnerability, distinguish **errors from deliberate defection**, and clarify a representative's **authority** before treating their promises as commitments.

chunks.heading: Class results (anonymised)
chunks.text:
| Pair | Joint profit (10 rounds) | Pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Pair with the longest cooperation | 22,800 | Kept for eight rounds, defected at the end |
| Middle pair | 20,800 | Early defections, cooperation from round 7 |
| Pair with the lowest joint profit | 18,800 | Early defection, a long cut spiral, cooperation in the middle, end defection |

The maximum possible was 24,000 (both keep every round). **Every pair defected near the end** once the remaining rounds became visible.

chunks.heading: Case summary (internal)
chunks.text:
Internal summary for the coach and the roleplay simulator. Never shown or cited to the user.

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Situation | Repeated keep-or-cut pricing game between two bubble-tea stalls |
| Actors | Two teams, one per stall |
| Known information | The payoff table |
| Unknown information | The other team's intentions; when the game would end (until near the end) |
| BATNAs | Cut every round (800 per round guaranteed) |
| Offers | Moves and, later, spoken promises |
| Outcome | Joint profit 18,800–22,800 of a possible 24,000 |
| What worked / failed | Worked: talking and then keeping the promise. Failed: defensive cutting and predicted end-game defection |
| Focus | Joint profit and the pattern over time |
| Do not disclose | n/a: cooperation needed openness |
| Do disclose | Intentions early, and a plan for the final rounds |
| Rules illustrated | RULE-038, RULE-037, RULE-009 (see Decision-Rules) |

chunks.heading: Lessons for the salary chatbot
chunks.text:
1. **Salary talks are repeated games.** The user will work with the manager afterwards, so short-term "wins" can cost later (Repeated-Games-and-End-Effects).
2. **End effects are real:** a user who is leaving is in an end game; an employer may behave differently with someone they expect to stay.
3. **Follow through on promises** ("I'll send the evidence by Friday"): deeds build credibility (Trust-and-Reciprocity).
4. **Check authority:** a recruiter's promise is not the manager's commitment (Ratification-and-Authority).

A business graduate with no experience has a first offer as a junior analyst at a mid-sized company. Path A, offer received; stage position moving to numbers; modifier `first_job_or_graduate`.

All figures are **illustrative** (monthly gross SEK) and are not market data.

chunks.heading: Situation
chunks.text:
| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Actors | The user; a friendly recruiter who decides with approval from a hiring manager |
| Known information | Role junior analyst `[user]`; no experience `[user]`; base 34,000 `[user]` |
| Unknown information | Pension, vacation, notice, deadline; the user's own target; the recruiter's real ceiling |
| BATNA | None yet; the user is still applying elsewhere `[user]` |
| Offers so far | One offer, 34,000 |

chunks.heading: What the user asks
chunks.text: > "I got my first job offer: 34,000 a month as a junior analyst. Should I just accept? I don't want to seem ungrateful."

chunks.heading: Rules applied
chunks.text:
- RULE-016: do not accept the first offer on the spot; RULE-045: be ready to say yes to a written offer that meets the target.
- RULE-046: if you do not ask, you do not get.
- RULE-004: aim as high as evidence allows, and ask for the user's own target **before** showing market data.
- RULE-054: value the whole package, not only base pay.
- RULE-038: the relationship continues, so the ask is warm.
- Checks 2, 3, 4 and 6 in Recommendation-Checks.

chunks.heading: Coach reply
chunks.text:
> Congratulations, that is good news. Nothing has to be decided today: asking for a few days to look at the whole package is normal, and so is asking for more.
>
> Before I show any market data, two questions so that we aim properly:
> 1. What outcome would you be happy with, and why?
> 2. What else is in the offer: pension, vacation days, notice period and when they need an answer?
>
> *Based on: not accepting a first offer on the spot, whole-package value.*

chunks.heading: Numbers
chunks.text:
After the user answers (illustrative):

- Own target 37,000 `[user]`; offer 34,000 `[user]`.
- Market range for junior analysts: P25 33,000, median 35,500, P75 38,000, confidence medium, from a union pay statistic with quartiles, valid as of the date shown `[researcher]`.
- Gap to target: 3,000, about 8.8 percent of the offer `[computed]`.
- Target is inside the range and below P75, so no evidence flag `[computed]`.
- Anchor options from the engine: hold at 37,000, halfway to P75 at 37,500, or at P75 38,000 `[computed]`.

chunks.heading: Disclose and do not disclose
chunks.text:
- Say: keen on the role, glad about the offer, would like to talk about the base salary and one non-pay item.
- Do not say: the floor, that this is the only offer, that the user will accept anything.

chunks.heading: When the advice changes
chunks.text:
- If the market median is already at or below the offer, fewer asks; focus on non-pay terms.
- If the user has another real offer, move to the competing-offer modifier.
- If the recruiter wants an answer today, follow the deadline guidance in Ask-for-Time.

chunks.heading: Common failure
chunks.text: Giving a number before asking the user's own target, or telling the user to "accept gratefully". Both skip the evidence and the user's ownership.

A specialist with eight years of experience gets an offer from a company where HR says pay follows a grade. Path A, offer received; stage strategy; modifier `fixed_scale`.

All figures are **illustrative** (monthly gross SEK) and are not market data.

chunks.heading: Situation
chunks.text:
| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Actors | The user; an HR partner; the hiring manager who must approve exceptions |
| Known information | Offer 52,000 at level 3 `[user]`; HR says the range for the level is fixed `[user]` |
| Unknown information | The range limits; what places a person in the range; whether level 4 exists for the role |
| BATNA | The current job, comfortable, no pressure `[user]` |
| Offers so far | 52,000, 25 vacation days, occupational pension under the agreement |

chunks.heading: What the user asks
chunks.text: > "HR says the band for this level is fixed, so there is nothing to negotiate. Is that true?"

chunks.heading: Rules applied
chunks.text:
- RULE-049: when told it is not negotiable, ask why.
- RULE-057: prepare non-price options in advance.
- RULE-018: justify with independent standards, here the level criteria and market data.
- RULE-009: find out who decides, here the hiring manager above HR.
- RULE-054: whole package.
- Checks 4, 5, 6 and 8.

chunks.heading: Coach reply
chunks.text:
> A fixed band often means a fixed range, not a fixed number. Two things are worth finding out:
> 1. What are the lowest and highest figures for this level, and what decides where in the range a person lands?
> 2. Does the role include responsibility that fits the level above, and who could approve a different level?
>
> Pension and vacation are usually set by the agreement, but a review date, a development budget and flexibility often are not. We can build the ask around those if base pay is capped.
>
> *Based on: asking why when told no, non-price options.*
>
> *Svenska:* Ett fast spann betyder ofta ett fast intervall, inte ett fast belopp. Två saker är värda att ta reda på: 1. Vilka är lägsta och högsta belopp för nivån, och vad avgör var i spannet man hamnar? 2. Innehåller rollen ansvar som motsvarar nivån över, och vem kan godkänna en annan nivå? Pension och semester följer ofta avtalet, men översynsdatum, utvecklingsbudget och flexibilitet gör det ofta inte.

chunks.heading: Numbers
chunks.text:
Illustrative:

- Level 3 range 48,000 to 56,000 `[user]`; offer 52,000 is the middle of the range `[computed]`.
- Market range for the role: P25 51,000, median 55,000, P75 59,000, confidence medium `[researcher]`. The offer is below the median by 3,000, about 5.5 percent `[computed]`.
- Evidence points to the upper half of the range or to level 4.

chunks.heading: Disclose and do not disclose
chunks.text:
- Say: the experience and the scope that fit the higher placement, and the market data with its source.
- Do not say: the walk-away or that the current job is comfortable.

chunks.heading: When the advice changes
chunks.text:
- If the range is genuinely one number (a public agreement), switch to Pay-Set-by-Agreement and focus on placement criteria and non-pay terms.
- If the user lacks level-4 scope, do not argue for it; use the market data for the top of the range.

chunks.heading: Common failure
chunks.text: Accepting "fixed" at face value, or arguing about fairness instead of asking what decides placement.

A candidate has two real offers. The preferred company says its offer is final and wants an answer by Friday. Path A, offer received; stage strategy; modifier `competing_offer`.

All figures are **illustrative** (monthly gross SEK) and are not market data.

chunks.heading: Situation
chunks.text:
| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Actors | The user; a recruiter under time pressure |
| Known information | Offer 1: 60,000, deadline Friday `[user]`. Offer 2: 56,000 plus three extra vacation days and a larger development budget, written `[user]` |
| Unknown information | Whether the Friday deadline is firm; how far offer 1 can move |
| BATNA | Offer 2 `[user]` |
| Offers so far | Two |

chunks.heading: What the user asks
chunks.text: > "They say 60,000 is final and I must answer by Friday. I prefer this job but the other offer has better extras. How do I use it?"

chunks.heading: Rules applied
chunks.text:
- RULE-001: a stronger BATNA gives more power; RULE-034: count only real alternatives; offer 2 is written, so it counts.
- RULE-020: signal options, not desperation.
- RULE-019 and RULE-044: never lie and never invent; state the other offer only as it is.
- RULE-016: do not accept on the spot; RULE-029: share priorities, protect the walk-away.
- RULE-026 and RULE-058: put the issues on one scale, introduced by purpose.
- Checks 3, 9 and 10.

chunks.heading: Coach reply
chunks.text:
> A real, written alternative is your strongest lever, so the way you use it matters. Two questions:
> 1. Is offer 2 in writing, and until when is it open?
> 2. If you could improve one thing in offer 1, would it be pay, vacation or development?
>
> A calm version could be: "I'm glad to get this offer and I'd like to join. I have another written offer with a different mix. Could we look at base pay and development, and could I have until {{date}} to decide?" That is true and does not reveal your floor.
>
> *Based on: using a real alternative honestly, asking for time.*

chunks.heading: Numbers
chunks.text:
- Difference in base: 4,000, about 7.1 percent of offer 2's base `[computed]`.
- Extras in offer 2 are listed beside the base and valued by the user with the points comparison, not by the coach.
- The walk-away is derived from offer 2 as the BATNA and is not shown to the recruiter `[user]`.

chunks.heading: Disclose and do not disclose
chunks.text:
- Say: that there is a real written alternative, in general terms, and the issues the user wants to discuss.
- Do not say: the walk-away, the exact terms of offer 2 unless it helps, or that the user will leave (unless true).

chunks.heading: When the advice changes
chunks.text:
- If offer 2 is only verbal or uncertain, treat the BATNA as weaker and do not lean on it.
- If the deadline is firm and offer 1 does not move, the user decides with the points comparison; the coach does not decide for them.

chunks.heading: Common failure
chunks.text: Inventing or inflating the other offer, or revealing that the user prefers this job.

A product manager gets an offer from an early-stage company with a lower salary and share options. Path A, offer received; stage position; modifier `equity_heavy`.

All figures are **illustrative** (monthly gross SEK) and are not market data.

chunks.heading: Situation
chunks.text:
| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Actors | The user; a founder who decides |
| Known information | Base 44,000 `[user]`; options for 0.2 percent of the shares, four-year vesting with a one-year cliff `[user]` |
| Unknown information | Strike price, number of shares outstanding, terms on exit or leaving, the company's funding |
| BATNA | Current job, stable `[user]` |
| Offers so far | Base 44,000 plus options |

chunks.heading: What the user asks
chunks.text: > "Are the options worth it? The founder says they could be big."

chunks.heading: Rules applied
chunks.text:
- RULE-054: value the whole package; D69: facts and employer cost only, the user decides what the options are worth.
- RULE-044: never invent facts, so no value is made up for the options.
- RULE-019: when unsure, say so; the hard rule on answers without backing applies, so any view is a labelled guess.
- RULE-057 and RULE-024: ask for what is cheap for the company, such as a review date or more cash later.
- Checks 2 and 6.

chunks.heading: Coach reply
chunks.text:
> I can't put a value on the options, because that depends on terms we don't know yet.
>
> **Guess, certainty low, and it may be wrong:** early-stage options are often worth little or nothing, with a few cases worth a lot. Treat them as an upside, not as part of your salary. If you'd like something more certain, I can check how options are usually described and taxed.
>
> Two things to find out first:
> 1. What is the strike price, how many shares are outstanding, and what happens to vested options if you leave?
> 2. How much do you need from the cash salary to be comfortable?
>
> *Based on: whole-package value, equity as upside.*

chunks.heading: Numbers
chunks.text:
- Base 44,000 `[user]`; market median for the role 46,500, confidence low (thin data) `[researcher]`.
- Gap: 2,500, about 5.4 percent of the median `[computed]`.
- Options: base case valued at 0, upside shown separately and never added `[assumed]`.
- Tax on options is a specialist matter; the coach points to Employee-Options-and-Equity and a tax adviser.

chunks.heading: Disclose and do not disclose
chunks.text:
- Say: interest in the vision, and questions about terms.
- Do not say: how much equity would change the user's decision, or the walk-away.

chunks.heading: When the advice changes
chunks.text:
- If the terms are good and the user's cash need is low, the equity may be a reason to accept a lower base; that choice is the user's.
- If the founder cannot answer basic terms, treat the equity as zero and negotiate the cash.

chunks.heading: Common failure
chunks.text: Putting a figure on the options, or telling the user that the equity "makes up for" the lower cash.

An analyst with a strong year has the yearly salary conversation in three weeks. Path B, annual review; stage position, moving to numbers.

All figures are **illustrative** (monthly gross SEK) and are not market data.

chunks.heading: Situation
chunks.text:
| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Actors | The user; a supportive line manager who takes cases to HR |
| Known information | Base 48,000 `[user]`; last raise 14 months ago `[user]`; three results with figures `[user]`; review in three weeks `[user]` |
| Unknown information | The raise pool and when budgets are fixed; the manager's view of the market |
| BATNA | Weak: no active search `[user]` |
| Offers so far | None |

chunks.heading: What the user asks
chunks.text: > "My review is in three weeks. I had a good year. What should I ask for?"

chunks.heading: Rules applied
chunks.text:
- RULE-046: if you do not ask, you do not get; RULE-004: aim as high as evidence allows; the user's own target comes first.
- RULE-018: justify with independent standards (results and market data).
- RULE-006: show what replacing the user would cost.
- RULE-039: frame the ask around the employer's gain.
- Checks 2, 4, 5 and 8; check 1 shapes the tone because the relationship continues.

chunks.heading: Coach reply
chunks.text:
> You have a good basis. Two things to settle first:
> 1. What would you be happy with after this review, and why?
> 2. When does your company fix next year's pay budget? If it is soon, we should raise this early.
>
> Then we'll go through the year month by month so that we catch everything you've done, not only the three results, and pick the strongest points for the conversation. I'll check where your pay sits against the market after you've given your own number.
>
> *Based on: asking as high as the evidence allows, timing against the budget cycle.*

chunks.heading: Numbers
chunks.text:
- Base 48,000 `[user]`. Market median for the role 51,000, confidence medium `[researcher]`.
- Gap to the median: 3,000, about 5.9 percent of the median `[computed]`.
- After the user names a target (for example 52,000 `[user]`), the engine checks it against P75 (for example 55,000 `[researcher]`) and returns no evidence flag `[computed]`.

chunks.heading: Disclose and do not disclose
chunks.text:
- Say: the results with numbers and what the user wants next.
- Do not say: the walk-away or that the user has no alternatives.

chunks.heading: When the advice changes
chunks.text:
- If the raise pool is already fixed, shift to a dated review and non-pay terms.
- If the user cannot quantify any result, run the evidence interview first.

chunks.heading: Common failure
chunks.text: Asking for "a bit more" with no number and no evidence, or waiting until the budget is fixed.

A consultant has taken over a small team and a client area in the past year and wants a raise and a new title. The manager is sceptical. Path B, promotion or role change; stage strategy; modifier `promotion_or_title`.

All figures are **illustrative** (monthly gross SEK) and are not market data.

chunks.heading: Situation
chunks.text:
| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Actors | The user; a sceptical manager; HR for title changes |
| Known information | Base 55,000 `[user]`; same title for two years `[user]`; team of three and a client area `[user]` |
| Unknown information | The manager's criteria for the title; the budget |
| BATNA | Moderate: recruiters have contacted the user `[user]` |
| Offers so far | None |

chunks.heading: What the user asks
chunks.text: > "My manager says good performance is expected and that a title change is premature. What do I say?"

chunks.heading: Rules applied
chunks.text:
- RULE-018 and RULE-040: independent standards and one concrete story per key claim.
- RULE-039: frame the ask around the team's gain.
- RULE-051: answer internal-equity concerns with uniqueness and cost.
- RULE-050: if they cannot justify a yes now, make it conditional; RULE-027: bridge doubts with if-then terms.
- RULE-047: not now, not no.
- Checks 5, 7 and 10.

chunks.heading: Coach reply
chunks.text:
> Agree with the manager's point, and then change the question. Two things to ask:
> 1. What would the role need to look like, in your manager's view, for the new title?
> 2. Which of your results can you show with a number or a client's written feedback?
>
> A possible line: "Good performance is the baseline. What has changed is the scope: I now lead three people and own the {{client area}}. What would you need to see to move my pay and title to match?" If the answer is "later", propose a dated review with named criteria.
>
> *Based on: independent standards, conditional agreements.*

chunks.heading: Numbers
chunks.text:
- Base 55,000 `[user]`. For the larger role the market median is 60,000, confidence low because data is thin `[researcher]`.
- Gap: 5,000, about 9.1 percent of the current base `[computed]`.
- The low confidence is stated in the brief; a figure is not forced.

chunks.heading: Disclose and do not disclose
chunks.text:
- Say: the scope facts and the question about criteria.
- Do not say: comparisons with named colleagues or the recruiter contacts as a threat.

chunks.heading: When the advice changes
chunks.text:
- If the manager gives clear criteria, build the case against them.
- If the manager cannot name any, escalate gently to a dated review with HR present.

chunks.heading: Common failure
chunks.text: Arguing that the user "deserves" it, or demanding both pay and title with no criteria.

A user in Sweden writes in Swedish; the manager says there is no money for raises this year. The reply follows the language toggle. Path B, annual review; stage strategy.

All figures are **illustrative** (monthly gross SEK) and are not market data.

chunks.heading: Situation
chunks.text:
| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Actors | The user; a manager with a small pool |
| Known information | Base 42,000 `[user]`; pool about 1.5 percent `[user]`; the user values flexibility and development `[user]` |
| Unknown information | Whether an exception is possible; the next budget date |
| BATNA | Moderate `[user]` |
| Offers so far | None |

chunks.heading: What the user asks
chunks.text: > "Min chef säger att det inte finns någon budget i år. Ska jag bara acceptera det?"

chunks.heading: Rules applied
chunks.text:
- RULE-049: when told it is not possible, ask why.
- RULE-057 and RULE-024: prepared non-price options; trade what is cheap for them for what is valuable to you.
- RULE-050 and RULE-027: if they cannot say yes now, make it conditional with a dated review.
- RULE-038: the relationship continues.
- RULE-054: whole package.
- Checks 7 and 10.

chunks.heading: Coach reply
chunks.text:
> Det är värt att fråga vidare istället för att acceptera direkt. Två frågor:
> 1. Vad skulle du helst vilja ha om lönen inte kan ändras, till exempel flexibilitet, utbildning eller en tydlig utvecklingsplan?
> 2. När sätts nästa budget, och vad skulle behöva vara uppfyllt för en översyn då?
>
> En möjlig formulering: "Jag förstår att potten är liten. Kan vi komma överens om {{utvecklingsinsats}} nu, och sätta ett datum i {{månad}} då vi tittar på lönen igen utifrån {{kriterier}}?"
>
> *Grundat på: fråga varför, villkorade överenskommelser, förslag i paket.*
>
> *English gloss:* Worth asking further rather than accepting at once. Find out what the user would most want if pay cannot change, and when the next budget is set; propose a development item now and a dated review with criteria.

chunks.heading: Numbers
chunks.text:
- Base 42,000 `[user]`; pool about 1.5 percent gives about 630 `[computed]`.
- The coach does not claim a value for the non-pay items; the user rates them with the points comparison if they want a ranking.

chunks.heading: Disclose and do not disclose
chunks.text:
- Say: the interest in flexibility and development, and the wish for a dated review.
- Do not say: the walk-away or any threat to leave.

chunks.heading: When the advice changes
chunks.text:
- If the market shows the user is clearly underpaid, ask for a one-off adjustment on the evidence.
- If the company is struggling, the dated review matters more than any amount.

chunks.heading: Common failure
chunks.text: Replying only in English to a Swedish message, or pushing for base pay against a clear budget limit with no other option.

A municipal administrator is told that pay follows the collective agreement and local pay criteria. Path B, annual review; stage strategy; modifier `fixed_scale`. Swedish agreement facts are time-sensitive and checked before use.

All figures are **illustrative** (monthly gross SEK) and are not market data.

chunks.heading: Situation
chunks.text:
| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Actors | The user; a manager in a public organisation; HR; the union representative |
| Known information | Base 41,000 `[user]`; public employer `[user]`; local pay criteria exist `[user]` |
| Unknown information | The criteria; what the user can show against them; the next pay-review date |
| BATNA | Weak; the user prefers to stay `[user]` |
| Offers so far | None |

chunks.heading: What the user asks
chunks.text: > "Pay is set by the agreement here, so my manager says there is no room. Is there anything I can do?"

chunks.heading: Rules applied
chunks.text:
- RULE-049: ask why and what decides the outcome.
- RULE-018: independent standards, here the published criteria.
- RULE-051: uniqueness and cost.
- RULE-057: non-price options.
- RULE-050: a dated review with criteria.
- Check 8: who decides, which may be the manager, HR or a pay-review committee.

chunks.heading: Coach reply
chunks.text:
> Even under an agreement, pay usually depends on criteria such as the level of responsibility and how the work is judged. Two things to find out:
> 1. Which agreement and which local pay criteria apply, and where in the pay range you sit now?
> 2. When is the next pay review, and what would you need to show by then?
>
> Your union representative can confirm what the agreement says. I can then help you line up your responsibilities against each criterion and ask for something concrete: a placement, a development plan or a dated review.
>
> *Based on: asking why when told no, independent standards. Agreement terms change; verify them with your union or HR before relying on them.*

chunks.heading: Numbers
chunks.text:
- Base 41,000 `[user]`. No market range is forced; public pay data is used only if the source gives it, and then with its date and confidence `[researcher]`.
- Any step in the range is computed only after the range is known `[computed]`.

chunks.heading: Disclose and do not disclose
chunks.text:
- Say: the criteria met and the responsibilities, not comparisons with named colleagues.
- Do not say: the walk-away or anything that blames the manager.

chunks.heading: When the advice changes
chunks.text:
- If the agreement allows an individual pay step, build the case for it.
- If the user is above the criteria, ask for a re-grade through the process.

chunks.heading: Common failure
chunks.text: Treating "set by the agreement" as the end of the conversation, or arguing as if pay were open to individual negotiation.

A running list of everything the user did that helped the employer, kept all year and used to build the case for a raise or promotion (B-Evidence-Builder). Collect widely, present narrowly: the full list goes into the brief appendix, three to five items go into the meeting.

chunks.heading: Entry format
chunks.text:
| Month | What I did (action) | Situation | Result and measure | Who benefited | Category | Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| {{month}} | {{ }} | {{ }} | {{number: SEK, %, hours, quality, risk}} | {{team, customer, company}} | {{see below}} | {{ }} |

chunks.heading: Categories to prompt for
chunks.text: Revenue and sales · cost savings and efficiency · customers and quality · projects delivered · new responsibility or scope · leadership and mentoring · process or tool improvements · knowledge and training · hard situations handled · recognition and feedback · extra hours or cover for others · work outside the job description.

chunks.heading: How the coach uses it
chunks.text:
- Ask the user to go through the year month by month and by category; do not stop at the first few.
- Ask for a number or fact on each item: "How would you measure it?" If none exists, an honest description is enough.
- Mark each item with a level: result achieved, scope grown, or effort only. Effort alone is weak evidence (Performance-Not-Enough).
- Pick three to five for the meeting; keep the rest in reserve (Story-vs-Statistics).
- Keep updating it after the meeting for the next round (B-Follow-Up-Plan).

chunks.heading: Rules
chunks.text:
- Only things the user says they did; the coach never invents or inflates an achievement.
- No colleagues' names or private information in the document.
- The user owns the list; nothing is stored by the product after the session.

chunks.heading: How the coach uses it
chunks.text:
- Start with what was agreed and make sure it is written down (Summarise-and-Confirm).
- Compare with the plan in Prep-Sheet, neutrally and without blame.
- If the answer was no or below the floor, move to B-When-the-Answer-Is-No and plan the next step.
- Update the evidence list for the next round (B-Follow-Up-Plan).
- A debrief is not a verdict on the user. Name one thing that went well.

chunks.heading: Rules for the coach
chunks.text:
- Do not reconstruct what was said if the user is unsure; ask them to confirm with the other side in writing.
- Time-sensitive facts from the session (decision date, expiry) are re-confirmed (Pre-Meeting-Checklist).

A scoring system puts different issues on **one metric** so the user can compare packages and see what to trade. Use it for a job offer, for a salary package at the current job, or for building MESO packages (Present-MESO-Packages). Method and theory are in Scoring-Systems.

chunks.heading: Steps
chunks.text:
1. **List the issues** (base salary, bonus, pension, vacation, flexibility, development, title, location, stability, equity). Add non-pay factors: the work, the team, the promotion schedule.
2. **Weights:** give each issue a weight. The weights must add up to **100%**.
3. **Options:** for each issue, list the plausible outcomes (for example 52 000, 55 000, 58 000 SEK).
4. **Values:** give each option a value from 0 to 100 (the best option on that issue is 100).
5. **Score a package:** add up weight × value over all issues.
6. **Compare packages.**
7. **Check:** does the ranking feel right? If not, adjust the weights or values and run it again.

chunks.heading: Template
chunks.text:
| Issue | Weight (%) | Option | Value (0-100) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base salary | | | |
| | | | |
| Bonus | | | |
| | | | |
| Pension | | | |
| Vacation | | | |
| Flexibility / remote | | | |
| Development | | | |
| Title or role | | | |
| Other: | | | |
| **Total weights** | **100** | | |

Then for each package: Score = sum of (weight ÷ 100 × value).

chunks.heading: Example (illustrative; not real market data)
chunks.text:
Weights: base salary 50%, flexibility 30%, vacation 20%.

| Issue | Weight | Option | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base salary (SEK/month gross) | 50% | 58 000 | 100 |
| | | 55 000 | 75 |
| | | 52 000 | 50 |
| Flexibility | 30% | 3 remote days | 100 |
| | | 1 remote day | 60 |
| | | Office only | 20 |
| Vacation | 20% | +5 days | 100 |
| | | +2 days | 70 |
| | | Standard | 50 |

| Package | Base | Flexibility | Vacation | Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 55 000 (75) | 3 remote days (100) | Standard (50) | 77.5 |
| 2 | 58 000 (100) | Office only (20) | +5 days (100) | 76.0 |
| 3 | 52 000 (50) | 3 remote days (100) | +5 days (100) | 75.0 |

The packages score almost the same for this user, so all three could be offered as equivalent options. Differences this small mean the user is close to indifferent: look at which package the employer finds cheapest.

chunks.heading: Quick version (for a user who has never used one)
chunks.text: The coach does not need the user to know the term. It asks: "If you had 100 points to spend on these, how would you spend them?" and uses the answer as the weights. If the user cannot say, the coach asks them to rank the issues, and the numbers engine gives default points (three issues: 61, 28, 11; four issues: 52, 27, 15, 6) that the user can change. For issues measured in numbers, such as base salary, the engine rates the options on a straight line from the walk-away level (0) to the best option (100); the user can override any rating. See Package-Scoring-Guide.

chunks.heading: How the chatbot uses it
chunks.text: The numbers engine calculates the scores, so the arithmetic is exact. The coach introduces the sheet in plain words (Package-Scoring-Guide), helps the user choose weights and values, checks that they add up to 100, and uses the result to build two or three equivalent packages. See Numbers-Stage.

chunks.heading: Common mistakes
chunks.text:
- Giving most weight to what is easiest to quantify (base salary) rather than what matters.
- Weights that do not add up to 100%.
- Never recalibrating when the ranking feels wrong.

A planning document is a one-page chart that compares **you** and **the other side** on the basic concepts. Established practice recommends building one before every negotiation. It helps prepare systematically, helps you work with a partner (for example a union representative), and transfers the skills to real situations. Where you lack information about the other side, **guess**, and plan questions that test the guesses.

chunks.heading: Fill-in chart
chunks.text:
| | **You** | **The other side (guess)** |
|---|---|---|
| Interests: what matters most, in order | | |
| BATNA | | |
| Reservation price (walk-away) | | |
| Target | | |
| Sources of power | | |
| Weaknesses | | |
| Likely objections | | |

**Opening move:**

**Other important information (deadline, budget cycle, agreement, who decides):**

chunks.heading: Questions to prepare for the planning step
chunks.text:
Questions for the planning step:

- Have I researched salary ranges and what issues may come up?
- What are my priorities (financial, stability, location, independence, mental stimulation, personal growth, low stress)?
- Which issues are missing, which are compatible, and where can I trade?
- What are my sources of power?
- Why do I deserve my target offer?
- What is the least acceptable deal that still covers my interests?

| Other side | `counterpart`, `zopa_estimate` |

chunks.text:
- Use ranges and mark guesses with `[assumed]`.
- Keep it to one page.
- Do not show it to the other side.

A checklist for the days before a salary conversation or an offer answer. Section 8 of the prep brief (Output-Templates) draws its items from here; the coach picks the ones that fit the situation and shows at most eight.

chunks.heading: Always
chunks.text:
- [ ] I know my walk-away, target and opening figure, and I can say them out loud (Prep-Sheet).
- [ ] I have my three to five points with a number or fact behind each.
- [ ] I have written my opening sentence and practised it once.
- [ ] I know what I will say if the answer is no, and what I will ask for instead.
- [ ] I know who decides and when the decision is made.
- [ ] I have a plan for the end of the meeting: what is agreed, by whom, by when.
- [ ] I will take notes, or ask to confirm the summary in writing (Summarise-and-Confirm).

chunks.heading: Path B (yearly review)
chunks.text:
- [ ] The meeting is booked early enough to matter for the pay round.
- [ ] I have checked my market position against a range with a source and a date.
- [ ] My results from the year are written down, including ones I will not use in the meeting.
- [ ] I know whether a collective agreement or a pay scale limits what can be changed.

chunks.heading: Path A (offer)
chunks.text:
- [ ] I have the offer in writing, with every component and the date it expires.
- [ ] I have compared it with my current job and any other offer.
- [ ] I have a list of the open terms: probation, notice period, non-compete, pension, variable pay.
- [ ] After agreeing, I will ask for the final terms in writing before I resign (A-Accepting-and-Confirming-in-Writing).

chunks.heading: Right after
chunks.text:
- [ ] Send a short thank-you and summary the same day or the next.
- [ ] Fill in Debrief-Sheet while it is fresh.

chunks.heading: Rules for the coach
chunks.text:
- Offer, do not order: the user decides what to tick.
- Never add an item that would require a false statement or pressure.
